nah.note: Kept existing draft. Molina 1571 'ocelotl: tigre'; Karttunen 1983 ocēlōtl. Also a day sign of the tonalpohualli, but the everyday animal noun; not a deity name.
nah.headword: Molina 1571 s.v. ocelotl; cf. Karttunen 1983 (from memory; page not checked)

yua.note: Changed from existing draft 'balam' (colonial/Classic spelling) to show the long vowel of modern Yucatec, written báalam with tone in Bricker et al. 1998 and Bastarrachea et al. Diccionario básico. Alternative: chak mo'ol (also cited for jaguar/puma; regional). Association: balamo'ob are also guardian spirits of milpa and village in traditional belief; the animal sense is ordinary everyday usage, but reviewers should confirm it reads as the animal for children.
yua.headword: báalam (Bricker et al. 1998) (from memory; page not verified)

quz.note: Uturunku is the jaguar (Panthera onca), source of Peruvian Spanish 'otorongo'. NOT 'puma', which is the cougar (Puma concolor) and would be a different animal; do not substitute. Jaguars are lowland (Amazonian) animals, so highland children may know the word mainly from stories; the uturunku is a prominent Inca/Andean symbolic animal (also in 'uturunku achachi' legends), but the plain noun is everyday vocabulary. Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976).
quz.headword: uturunku (AMLQ 2005 / Cusihuamán 1976 headword form, from memory; page not verified)

cjp.note: General (unmarked) form. d.n. synonym satálá (entry 5405). SENSITIVE: the jaguar has ritual weight in Cabécar practice; the dictionary lists na_má_ bata (ceremonial helper, 4517) and na_má_ dalí 'enfermedad del tigre', a taboo-linked illness (4518). Plain noun is everyday vocabulary.
cjp.reviewQuestion: ¿Se usa 'na̱má̱' para el jaguar con niños sin problema, o prefieren 'satálá' (Chirripó)?

bzd.note: Everyday noun for jaguar (Panthera onca). Synonym dulë́kalöm (variants dulë́kalö, dulë́klöm) per Margery 1996/Flores 2009. Variant spelling nmù̱. Sensitivity: the jaguar figures in Bribri narratives and is associated with a clan (Tùbölwak, per Jara & García 2003); the plain animal noun is ordinary vocabulary, but avoid compounds like na̱mù̱ dalë̀ ('jaguar sickness').
bzd.source: jaragarcia2013; margery1996; flores2009 (as indexed in Krohn 2025 online dictionary, ES→BRI entry 'jaguar'; primary page not verified)
bzd.reviewQuestion: Is na̱mù̱ the word children would use for the jaguar picture, or dulë́kalöm? Which do you prefer for a game?

verso.es:
Manchas de luz entre la selva,
el jaguar camina sin hacer ruido.
verso.en:
Spots of light among the trees,
the jaguar walks without a sound.

riddle.es: Soy gato grande de la selva y llevo la noche pintada en la piel.
riddle.en: I am the big cat of the jungle, and I wear the night painted on my coat.

nah.note: Kept existing draft. Molina 'huitzitzilin: pájaro pequeño de pluma rica'; Karttunen huitzitzilin. Root of the deity name Huitzilopochtli, but the bird noun itself is ordinary.
nah.headword: Molina 1571 s.v. huitzitzilin; cf. Karttunen 1983 (from memory; page not checked)

yua.note: Kept existing draft. Widely documented (Bricker et al. 1998; Diccionario básico; Cordemex). Tone/length marking varies across sources (ts'unu'un vs ts'úunu'un).
yua.headword: ts'unu'un (Bricker et al. 1998) (from memory; page not verified)

quz.note: Common word for hummingbird; AMLQ spells it 'q'enti' (with e allophone written). Pronounced with e near q. Name also appears in place names (Q'intiq…). Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976).
quz.headword: q'enti (AMLQ 2005 / Cusihuamán 1976 headword form, from memory; page not verified)

cjp.note: Southern-dialect form. The northern (d.n.) generic is ma_tsu_ (entry ~4295), but the dictionary also gives ma_tsu_ (d.n., vulg.) 'pene' — avoided for a children's game. batsu_ is also a dog's name in San José Cabécar (SJC). Chirripó speakers may expect ma_tsu_.
cjp.reviewQuestion: ¿Cómo dicen 'colibrí' en su comunidad: 'batsu̱' o 'ma̱tsu̱'? ¿'ma̱tsu̱' tiene un doble sentido que no conviene para niños?

bzd.note: Generic for hummingbirds (Trochilidae); also 'small long-billed bird'. Variants bitsù̱, btsù̱. Many species compounds exist; avoid sibö̀batsu̱ (contains the sacred name Sibö̀).
bzd.source: jaragarcia2003; flores2009; margery1996; dipalicori_animales (as indexed in Krohn 2025 online dictionary, ES→BRI entry 'colibrí'; primary page not verified)
bzd.reviewQuestion: Is batsù̱ (or bitsù̱/btsù̱) how your community says it?

verso.es:
Pequeño como un suspiro,
bebe flores y no se detiene.
verso.en:
Small as a sigh,
it sips from flowers and never rests.

riddle.es: Mis alas zumban tan rápido que casi no se ven; me paro en el aire para beber néctar.
riddle.en: My wings hum so fast you can hardly see them; I hover in the air to sip nectar.

quz.note: Kept existing draft. Native Quechua word (source of the Spanish). Alternatives: 'qarwa' (llama, esp. pale/yellowish in some sources), 'llamas' plural is -kuna: 'llamakuna'. Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976).
quz.headword: llama (AMLQ 2005 / Cusihuamán 1976 headword form, from memory; page not verified)

nah.note: Spanish word, not traditional Nahuatl. Llamas are Andean; no native referent. ichcatl (cotton; post-contact "sheep") would mislead.
nah.reviewQuestion: ¿Se dice "llama" tal cual en náhuatl, o hay otra palabra que usen para este animal?

yua.note: Spanish loanword. The llama is Andean and not native to the peninsula; no traditional Yucatec word is expected. Medium only because it is clearly a loan; Spanish spelling kept per loan policy; pronunciation may be [jama]. Do not invent a native term. Alternative to review: keep Spanish spelling as a marked loan.
yua.reviewQuestion: For the Andean llama, do you use a Maya word or just say 'llama'? How do you pronounce it?

cjp.note: Andean animal with no Cabécar term in the dictionary. The Bible translation borrows Spanish names for foreign animals ('camello', 'oveja', 'cabra'), so a Spanish loan 'llama' is plausible, but it is unattested here; left null rather than guessed.
cjp.reviewQuestion: ¿Dirían simplemente 'llama' (en español) o hay otra forma?

bzd.note: No Bribri entry for the Andean llama; the animal is not native to Talamanca. No attested Bribri loan found. Do not substitute another animal.
bzd.reviewQuestion: Do children in your community use a Spanish loan for this (how is it pronounced/written in Bribri spelling), or is there a Bribri word or phrase?

verso.es:
Camina por la sierra alta
con su lana como nube.
verso.en:
It walks the high ridges
with wool like a cloud.

riddle.es: Vivo en los Andes, cargo con paciencia y mi lana abriga a todos.
riddle.en: I live in the Andes, I carry loads with patience, and my wool keeps everyone warm.

nah.note: Spanish word, not traditional Nahuatl. The Andean condor has no Classical name. A descriptive phrase huey tzopilotl (huey "great" + tzopilotl "vulture", Molina s.v. tzopilotl) was considered but would be coined for this deck, not traditional, so it is offered only as an alternative. cozcacuauhtli (king vulture) is a different bird and a day sign; avoided.
nah.reviewQuestion: ¿Cómo se dice "cóndor" en su variante: se usa la palabra española, o se diría algo como "huey tzopilotl"?

yua.note: Spanish loan (cóndor), kept in Spanish spelling per loan policy. Andean bird, not native to the region. Alternative descriptive: nojoch ch'oom 'big vulture' (nojoch 'big' + ch'oom 'vulture/zopilote', both attested), which is transparent but not an established name.
yua.reviewQuestion: Do you have any word for the condor, or would you say 'cóndor' (or something like nojoch ch'oom, 'big vulture')?

quz.note: Source of Spanish 'cóndor'. The condor is symbolically important (national emblem, ritual dances), but kuntur is the plain animal noun. Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976).
quz.headword: kuntur (AMLQ 2005 / Cusihuamán 1976 headword form, from memory; page not verified)

cjp.note: Not a Costa Rican bird; no entry. The closest native concept is olo 'zopilote' (vulture, Bible.is Mt 24:28) and an entry for 'zopilote rey' (king vulture), but neither is a condor. Left null.
cjp.reviewQuestion: ¿Usarían 'cóndor' prestado del español, o el nombre del zopilote rey?

bzd.note: No Bribri entry for the Andean condor. Related but DIFFERENT birds are attested: ölö́bulu / uchí (king vulture, Sarcoramphus papa), ölö́ (vulture, generic), pú̱ (raptor, generic). Using any of these would name a different animal, so left empty.
bzd.reviewQuestion: Is there a Bribri way to refer to the Andean condor, or would you accept ölö́bulu (king vulture) only if the card art is changed?

verso.es:
Sus alas abren el cielo
y el viento lo lleva alto.
verso.en:
Its wings open up the sky
and the wind carries it high.

riddle.es: Soy de las aves voladoras más grandes; planeo sobre las cumbres sin aletear.
riddle.en: I am one of the largest flying birds; I glide over the peaks without flapping.

nah.note: Molina 'papalotl: mariposa'; Karttunen pāpālōtl. Widely kept in modern varieties (papalotl/papalot). Source of Mexican Spanish papalote (kite). papalotl sounds close to papa; avoidWith set.
nah.headword: Molina 1571 s.v. papalotl; cf. Karttunen 1983 (from memory; page not checked)

yua.note: Standard word, written péepem with tone (Bricker et al. 1998; Diccionario básico). Also used for moths.
yua.headword: péepem (Bricker et al. 1998) (from memory; page not verified)

quz.note: Standard Cusco word for butterfly; variant 'pilpintu'. Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976); Hornberger & Hornberger, Diccionario tri-lingüe Quechua of Cusco (1983).
quz.headword: pillpintu (AMLQ 2005 / Cusihuamán 1976 headword form, from memory; page not verified)

cjp.note: General form. d.n. variant kuák'a (3950, marked p.u. 'poco usado'). Night moths: kuákua yee (d.n.) 'mariposa nocturna'.

bzd.note: Generic for butterflies/moths (Lepidoptera). Variants kuàkua, short form kua’. Blue morpho is dulùkuékua. Also shown in the DIPALICORI animals dictionary as kua’kua / kuâkua.
bzd.source: jaragarcia2013; margery1996; jaragarcia2003; dipalicori_animales (as indexed in Krohn 2025 online dictionary, ES→BRI entry 'mariposa'; primary page not verified)
bzd.reviewQuestion: Is kua’kua the everyday form, and which tone/spelling do you prefer (kua’kua vs kuàkua)?

verso.es:
Viaja lejos, ligera y naranja,
y vuelve cuando florece el campo.
verso.en:
It travels far, light and orange,
and returns when the fields bloom.

riddle.es: De oruga me hice alas de colores y cruzo países volando.
riddle.en: I was a caterpillar once; now I have colored wings and fly across countries.

nah.note: Molina 'huexolotl: gallo de la tierra'; source of Spanish guajolote. totolin is the generic/hen term and an alternative; the card shows a displaying male, so huexolotl fits.
nah.headword: Molina 1571 s.v. huexolotl; cf. Karttunen 1983 (from memory; page not checked)

yua.note: úulum = domestic turkey (Bricker et al. 1998; Cordemex ulum). The wild ocellated turkey of the peninsula is kuuts, a different bird; the card shows the gobbling domestic turkey. Association: turkeys are offered in some traditional ceremonies; the word itself is everyday.
yua.headword: úulum (Bricker et al. 1998) (from memory; page not verified)

quz.note: Turkey is a Mesoamerican domesticate with no native Andean name I can confirm. 'pawu' is a Spanish loan ('pavo') adapted to Quechua phonology; speakers may simply say 'pavo'. Do not confuse with native Andean birds (e.g. 'pawa' / guan, uncertain). Needs native-speaker check of what is actually said.
quz.reviewQuestion: What do you call a turkey (the farmyard bird, Spanish 'pavo') when speaking Quechua — 'pawu', 'pavo', or another word?

cjp.note: General form. Short one-syllable word: check it is distinct enough in audio from other cho-/chö- words.

bzd.note: Domestic turkey; Costa Rican Spanish 'chompipe'. Nasal vowel ò̱ (macron below).
bzd.source: margery1996; rimolo2007 (as indexed in Krohn 2025 online dictionary, ES→BRI entry 'chompipe / pavo'; primary page not verified)
bzd.reviewQuestion: Is chò̱ used for the domestic turkey in your community?

verso.es:
Abre su cola como abanico
y presume con su glugluteo.
verso.en:
It fans its tail wide
and shows off with its gobble.

riddle.es: Tengo plumas de gala y hago glugluglú; vengo de estas tierras.
riddle.en: I wear fancy feathers, I go gobble-gobble, and my ancestors come from these lands.

nah.note: Molina 'ayotl: tortuga'; Karttunen āyōtl. RISK: without length marks it looks like ayohtli/ayotli 'squash'; reviewer may want a disambiguating spelling or diacritics.
nah.headword: Molina 1571 s.v. ayotl; cf. Karttunen 1983 (from memory; page not checked)

yua.note: áak 'turtle' (Cordemex; Bricker et al. 1998). Risk: near-homophones on this deck (aaktun cave, p'aak tomato) and elsewhere (ak' 'vine'); reviewers should confirm vowel length and the plain vs ejective k. Species names exist for sea vs land turtles; this is the general term. IPA ?.
yua.reviewQuestion: How do you say 'turtle': áak, aak, or ak? Is the vowel long? Could a child confuse it with áaktun (cave) or p'aak (tomato) when called aloud?
yua.headword: áak (Cordemex ac) (from memory; page not verified)

quz.note: Reviewer accepted: changed from 'charapa', which is a Peruvian-Amazon regional (probably not Quechua) word for the river turtle Podocnemis that I cannot defend as highland Cusco Quechua. Adapted Spanish loan per loan policy; speakers may say 'tortuga' unadapted.
quz.reviewQuestion: Is there a Quechua word you use for a turtle or tortoise, or do you say 'tortuga'? If the loan, how would you spell it?

cjp.note: General form kuë; Chirripó (d.n.) k'uë́ with glottalized k'. Tone mark on the general form not verified on the scan. Note: in the southern dialect kuë also means 'maíz' (entry ~4044) — homonym risk in a game that also has a maize card.
cjp.reviewQuestion: ¿Dicen 'kuë' o 'k'uë' para tortuga? ¿En su zona 'kuë' también es maíz?

bzd.note: Generic turtle. Sea turtles have specific names (sö̀ hawksbill, kakò̱ leatherback); freshwater turtle ö̀lëkuë / pó̱kuë. DIPALICORI animals dictionary shows 'sö / ölë kuë' on the turtles page.
bzd.source: margery1996; flores2009; dipalicori_animales (as indexed in Krohn 2025 online dictionary, ES→BRI entry 'tortuga'; primary page not verified)
bzd.reviewQuestion: For a generic turtle picture, is kuë̀ right, or would children name a specific kind?

verso.es:
Despacito, despacito,
llega lejos con su casa a cuestas.
verso.en:
Slowly, slowly,
it goes far with its home on its back.

riddle.es: Cargo mi casa en la espalda y avanzo sin prisa.
riddle.en: I carry my house on my back and go without hurry.

nah.note: Molina 'cueyatl: rana'; Karttunen cuēyatl. Modern forms vary (kueyatl, kuiyatl).
nah.headword: Molina 1571 s.v. cueyatl; cf. Karttunen 1983 (from memory; page not checked)

yua.note: much is the common word for toad, used loosely for frogs (Diccionario básico; Bricker); it may not cover the green frog of the card, hence low. wo' (uo), a rain-singing frog, is avoided as the card word because wo' frogs are part of the Ch'a' Cháak rain ceremony, where children imitate their calls.
yua.reviewQuestion: Is 'much' only a toad, or also a green frog like this picture? What do you call a green frog? Is wo' fine for children or tied to the rain ceremony?
yua.headword: much (Diccionario básico) (from memory; page not verified)

quz.note: Standard Cusco word for frog. Contrast 'hamp'atu' = toad; picture should be a frog. Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976).
quz.headword: k'ayra (AMLQ 2005 / Cusihuamán 1976 headword form, from memory; page not verified)

cjp.note: General form. Ch. variant yökok (p.u.). Do not confuse with buki/buke 'sapo' (toad, 647; Bible.is Rev 16:13 'buke'); buki also has a vulgar sense ('vulva', 647) — another reason to prefer bulbí.

bzd.note: Generic for frogs and toads. Variants bukë’ (used as the category label in the DIPALICORI animals dictionary) and bkuë’.
bzd.source: margery1996; flores2009; jaragarcia2003; dipalicori_animales (as indexed in Krohn 2025 online dictionary, ES→BRI entry 'rana'; primary page not verified)
bzd.reviewQuestion: Which form is used in your variety: bukuë’ or bukë’?

verso.es:
Salta, salta, croac, croac,
canta cuando llega la lluvia.
verso.en:
Jump, jump, ribbit, ribbit,
it sings when the rain arrives.

riddle.es: Soy verde y saltarina; en el charco canto después de la tormenta.
riddle.en: I am green and jumpy; by the puddle I sing after the storm.

nah.note: Molina 'coatl: culebra'; Karttunen cōātl. Ordinary noun; it is part of Quetzalcoatl and a day sign, but standing alone it is just 'snake'.
nah.headword: Molina 1571 s.v. coatl; cf. Karttunen 1983 (from memory; page not checked)

yua.note: kàan/káan 'snake' (Bricker et al. 1998). Do not confuse with ka'an 'sky' (glottal stop) or kaan 'four' in some spellings. Association: the feathered serpent K'uk'ulkan; the plain word is everyday.
yua.headword: kàan (Bricker et al. 1998) (from memory; page not verified)

quz.note: Ordinary word for snake (variant spelling mach'aqway / machaqway). Deliberately NOT 'amaru', which is the mythic/great serpent with strong religious and political associations. Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976). Reviewer flag accepted: the ejective is uncertain — sources vary between 'mach'aqway' and 'machaqway'. Shares 'mach'a-' with mach'ay (cueva), so avoidWith.
quz.reviewQuestion: Do you pronounce the word for snake with a popped (ejective) ch' — 'mach'aqway' — or plain 'machaqway'?
quz.headword: mach'aqway (AMLQ 2005 / Cusihuamán 1976 headword form, from memory; page not verified)

cjp.note: Bible spelling (matches MMS-TTS training text); dictionary writes tkabë, d.s. tkebë (6811), SJC chabe (734). Snakes are associated with healers/taboos in Cabécar tradition; neutral as a noun.
cjp.source: bibleis-cjptjv Mt 10:16, Lk 10:19 'tkäbe'; margery1989 entry 6784 tkabë (generic)

bzd.note: Generic snake. Krohn writes tk for a sound some speakers write tch (DIPALICORI uses tkabë / tchabë). Variant tkbë̀. Ritual-speech synonym tulít — do not use. Note tkabë̀ also means 'rainbow' (see arcoiris), linked to Bribri narratives.
bzd.source: jaragarcia2013; margery1996; dipalicori_animales (as indexed in Krohn 2025 online dictionary, ES→BRI entry 'serpiente'; primary page not verified)
bzd.reviewQuestion: Should the game spell this tkabë̀ or tchabë̀ for your community?

verso.es:
Sin patas va por el suelo,
deslizándose entre las piedras.
verso.en:
With no legs it travels the ground,
sliding between the stones.

riddle.es: No tengo patas pero avanzo; cambio de piel cuando crezco.
riddle.en: I have no legs but I move; I shed my skin when I grow.

nah.note: Kept existing draft. Molina 'centli: maçorca de maíz seca'. Alternatives: tlaolli (shelled kernels), elotl (green ear), cintli (variant spelling). Root of Centeotl, but the noun itself is everyday.
nah.headword: Molina 1571 s.v. centli; cf. Karttunen 1983 (from memory; page not checked)

yua.note: Kept existing draft. Standard word for maize grain (all major dictionaries). Related: nal 'ear of corn (fresh)'. Maize carries deep cultural and ritual weight, but ixi'im is the ordinary noun.
yua.headword: ixi'im (Bricker et al. 1998) (from memory; page not verified)

quz.note: Kept existing draft. Standard word for maize (plant and grain); 'choclo' (fresh ear) is 'chuqllu'. Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976).
quz.headword: sara (AMLQ 2005 / Cusihuamán 1976 headword form, from memory; page not verified)

cjp.note: Northern (Chirripó) form. Southern form kuë (d.s., ~4044) is homonymous with 'turtle'. Maize has ceremonial uses (chicha), but the word is everyday.
cjp.reviewQuestion: ¿'Ik'uö' es la forma usada en su comunidad para maíz?

bzd.note: Variants ikuö̀wö / ikuwö̀ (also 'maize grain') and kuwö̀. Many named varieties exist; avoid ritual-speech forms (sékibö etc.).
bzd.source: margery1996; jaragarcia2013 (as indexed in Krohn 2025 online dictionary, ES→BRI entry 'maíz'; primary page not verified)
bzd.reviewQuestion: Is ikuö̀ or ikuö̀wö the better word for a picture of an ear of corn?

verso.es:
Granitos de oro en su vaina,
del campo a la mesa.
verso.en:
Little golden grains in their husk,
from the field to the table.

riddle.es: De mí se hacen tortillas y tamales; tengo barba de seda y mil granos.
riddle.en: Tortillas and tamales are made from me; I have silky hair and a thousand kernels.

nah.note: Kept existing draft. Molina 'nopalli: tunal, árbol'. Source of Spanish nopal. Fruit is nochtli (tuna).
nah.headword: Molina 1571 s.v. nopalli; cf. Karttunen 1983 (from memory; page not checked)

yua.note: pak'am (also pak'an) 'nopal, tuna' in Cordemex and Diccionario básico. Final m vs n varies by source; reviewers should confirm. Opuntia occurs on the peninsula but is less culturally central than in central Mexico. IPA ?.
yua.reviewQuestion: How do you say 'nopal': pak'am or pak'an? Is it used for the plant, the fruit (tuna), or both?
yua.headword: pak'am (Cordemex pakam) (from memory; page not verified)

quz.gloss: prickly-pear fruit (Opuntia); the plant is uncertain
quz.note: Nopal is a Mexican term not used in Peru. In the Andes the Opuntia plant and fruit are called 'tuna', a word that entered via Spanish (originally Taíno), so it is labelled loanword. I do not know a confirmed native Quechua term; reviewers should check. Note the card art (nopal pads) may read as 'tuna' to Andean children. Reviewer point accepted: 'tuna' primarily names the fruit, not the pad/plant shown on the card.
quz.reviewQuestion: The card shows a prickly-pear cactus plant with flat pads. Does 'tuna' name the plant or only the fruit? Is there another word for the plant (e.g. 'waraqu' or similar)?

cjp.note: Opuntia is not part of the Talamanca/Chirripó environment; no entry. Left null.
cjp.reviewQuestion: ¿Existe un nombre cabécar para este cactus, o se usaría 'nopal'?

bzd.note: No Bribri entry for nopal (Opuntia), which is not a Talamanca plant. The only cactus entry is na̱mù̱yibala (Pereskia grandifolia), a different plant. No attested loan.
bzd.reviewQuestion: Do children in your community use a Spanish loan for this (how is it pronounced/written in Bribri spelling), or is there a Bribri word or phrase?

verso.es:
Raquetas verdes con espinas,
y tunas dulces al final.
verso.en:
Green paddles with prickly spines,
and sweet fruit at the end.

riddle.es: Soy cactus de hojas anchas; con cuidado me comen, y mi fruto es la tuna.
riddle.en: I am a cactus with wide pads; carefully, I am eaten, and my fruit is the prickly pear.

nah.note: Kept existing draft. Molina 'etl: frisol'; Karttunen ētl. Very short for a caller; reviewer may prefer a modern form (e.g. et, yetl in some varieties).
nah.headword: Molina 1571 s.v. etl; cf. Karttunen 1983 (from memory; page not checked)

yua.note: Kept existing draft. Standard word (all major dictionaries). Specific varieties have their own names (e.g. ib 'lima bean').
yua.headword: bu'ul (Bricker et al. 1998) (from memory; page not verified)

quz.note: Native word for bean, source of Southern Cone Spanish 'poroto'. Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976).
quz.headword: purutu (AMLQ 2005 / Cusihuamán 1976 headword form, from memory; page not verified)

cjp.note: General form; d.n./Uj. k'a_ní_ (3330) with glottalized k'. ka_ní_ kicharaga 'vainica' (green bean pod).

bzd.note: Common bean. Seed: átwö.
bzd.source: margery1996; sanchez_sf (as indexed in Krohn 2025 online dictionary, ES→BRI entry 'frijol'; primary page not verified)
bzd.reviewQuestion: Is átu the usual word for beans?

verso.es:
Trepa por la caña del maíz
y llena la olla de calor.
verso.en:
It climbs up the maize stalk
and fills the pot with warmth.

riddle.es: Vivo en una vaina y me cocino en la olla; con el maíz y la calabaza hago equipo.
riddle.en: I live in a pod and cook in the pot; with maize and squash I make a team.

nah.note: Spanish word, not traditional Nahuatl. I have a recollection of "matzatli" being given for pineapple, but I cannot name a dictionary or page for it, so it is unverified and not used.
nah.reviewQuestion: ¿Cómo se dice "piña" en su variante? ¿Conoce la palabra "matzatli" para la piña?

yua.note: Spanish loanword. I could not confirm a native Yucatec name for pineapple from sources I trust; rather than guess, this is left as a marked loan. Colonial dictionaries may record a native term; a reviewer should check Cordemex. Spanish spelling kept per loan policy.
yua.reviewQuestion: Is there a Maya word for pineapple, or do people just say 'piña'?

quz.note: Pineapple is a lowland fruit; speakers generally use Spanish 'piña'. Colonial sources record 'achupalla' for pineapple/bromeliads, but today achupalla refers mainly to wild Puya bromeliads, so it would confuse. Labelled loanword.
quz.reviewQuestion: For pineapple, do Quechua speakers say 'piña', or is 'achupalla' or another word used?

cjp.note: General form, two words as printed. Tone accents (í, ö́) as in the dictionary; MMS vocab has no combining acute so the accent on ö is dropped in synthesis.

bzd.note: Synonyms/variants: alàbawö, a̱mù̱wö, a̱mù̱wöli.
bzd.source: margery1996; sanchez_sf (as indexed in Krohn 2025 online dictionary, ES→BRI entry 'piña'; primary page not verified)
bzd.reviewQuestion: Which of abáwö / alàbawö / a̱mù̱wö is used in your community?

verso.es:
Corona de hojas verdes,
dulce corazón dorado.
verso.en:
A crown of green leaves,
a sweet golden heart.

riddle.es: Tengo corona de hojas y piel con picos; por dentro soy dulce y jugosa.
riddle.en: I wear a crown of leaves and have a spiky skin; inside I am sweet and juicy.

nah.note: Kept existing draft. Molina 'chilli: axí'; Karttunen chīlli.
nah.headword: Molina 1571 s.v. chilli; cf. Karttunen 1983 (from memory; page not checked)

yua.note: ìik/iik 'chile' (Bricker et al. 1998; Diccionario básico), as in x-ma'ax iik. Minimal pair with iik' 'wind' (ejective k') on the viento card; callers must pronounce the ejective clearly, and reviewers may want to flag this pair for children.
yua.headword: ìik (Bricker et al. 1998) (from memory; page not verified)

quz.note: Native generic word for Capsicum pepper (also 'hot spice'); the large rocoto is 'ruqut'u'. Domestic Andean Capsicum predates contact, so this is a genuine native word, not a Mesoamerican borrowing. Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976). Spelling of rocoto varies: 'ruqutu' vs 'ruqut'u'.
quz.headword: uchu (AMLQ 2005 / Cusihuamán 1976 headword form, from memory; page not verified)

cjp.note: General form. SJC dapa/dapo/dipa; Uj. baka shi 'chile de ganado'. One-syllable word.

bzd.gloss: chili pepper (sweet; also generic hot chili per Chevrier)
bzd.note: Primary sources gloss dipa’ as 'chile dulce' (Capsicum spp.); Chevrier 2017 also lists it as generic 'chile picante'. Variant dapa’; also sha’. Card shows a red hot chili.
bzd.source: margery1996; constenla2010; chevrier2017 (as indexed in Krohn 2025 online dictionary, ES→BRI entry 'chile'; primary page not verified)
bzd.reviewQuestion: Does dipa’ cover a hot red chili, or only sweet pepper? Is there a different word for the hot chili?

verso.es:
Rojo, verde, picoso,
hace llorar y hace sonreír.
verso.en:
Red, green, and fiery,
it makes you cry and makes you smile.

riddle.es: Soy pequeño y pico; en la salsa me conoces por el calor.
riddle.en: I am small and hot; in the salsa you know me by the heat.

quz.note: Kept existing draft. Native Quechua word (source of Spanish 'papa'). Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976).
quz.headword: papa (AMLQ 2005 / Cusihuamán 1976 headword form, from memory; page not verified)

nah.note: Spanish word, not traditional Nahuatl. Potato is Andean and post-contact in Mexico. Do NOT use camohtli (sweet potato, camote).
nah.reviewQuestion: ¿Se dice "papa" en náhuatl en su comunidad, o hay una palabra propia para la papa (no el camote)?

yua.note: Spanish loanword. Potato is Andean; no traditional Yucatec name expected. Do not substitute iis, which is sweet potato (camote), a different plant.
yua.reviewQuestion: Do people say 'papa' for potato in Maya, or another word?

cjp.note: Potato is not a traditional Cabécar crop. Spanish loan offered on the Bible.is precedent of keeping Spanish nouns for introduced items; not attested in Cabécar sources. Homophone risk: Spanish 'papá'.
cjp.source: no Cabécar term in margery1989 (only baga kiwö 'papa chiricana', a different tuber, entry 141)
cjp.reviewQuestion: ¿Dicen 'papa' en español para la papa, o hay otra palabra?

bzd.note: No Bribri entry for potato (Solanum tuberosum). Generic tu’ means 'tuber / yam' and would name a different food. No attested loan.
bzd.reviewQuestion: Do children in your community use a Spanish loan for this (how is it pronounced/written in Bribri spelling), or is there a Bribri word or phrase?

verso.es:
Crece bajo la tierra fría
y sale en mil formas y colores.
verso.en:
It grows beneath the cold soil
and comes in a thousand shapes and colors.

riddle.es: Nací en los Andes y vivo escondida bajo la tierra; hay de muchos colores.
riddle.en: I was born in the Andes and I hide underground; I come in many colors.

nah.note: Kept existing draft. Molina 'ahuacatl: fruta que llaman aguacate'; Karttunen āhuacatl. Note: also slang for testicle in Classical sources; harmless here but reviewer should be aware.
nah.headword: Molina 1571 s.v. ahuacatl; cf. Karttunen 1983 (from memory; page not checked)

yua.note: óon 'avocado' (Bricker et al. 1998; Cordemex on). Short, may need a clear call.
yua.headword: óon (Bricker et al. 1998) (from memory; page not verified)

quz.note: Andean word for avocado, source of Peruvian Spanish 'palta' (traditionally linked to the Palta people of southern Ecuador). Used by Quechua speakers but may be perceived as Spanish; origin debated. Do not confuse with 'p'alta' (flat), ejective. Mesoamerican origin of the fruit: Nahuatl 'ahuacatl' is unrelated.
quz.reviewQuestion: Is 'palta' felt as a Quechua word or as Spanish? Is there any other word for avocado?
quz.headword: palta (AMLQ 2005 / Cusihuamán 1976 headword form, from memory; page not verified)

cjp.note: General form; also jo_mó_ (2356) and d.n. a_mó_ (98). ja_mó_ klö́ = avocado tree.

bzd.note: Variants a̱mo̱’, mo̱’.
bzd.source: jara2018; chevrier2017 (as indexed in Krohn 2025 online dictionary, ES→BRI entry 'aguacate'; primary page not verified)
bzd.reviewQuestion: Is ja̱mo̱’ or a̱mo̱’ the form used for avocado in your community?

verso.es:
Verde por fuera, cremoso por dentro,
con un hueso grande de corazón.
verso.en:
Green outside, creamy inside,
with a big pit for a heart.

riddle.es: Mi pulpa es suave y verde y me untan en el pan; guardo un hueso grande.
riddle.en: My flesh is soft and green and spread on bread; I keep a big pit.

nah.note: CHANGED from existing draft tomatl. In central Mexico tomatl is mainly the green husk tomato (tomatillo); the red tomato on this card ('rojo y jugoso') is xitomatl (Molina/Karttunen; source of Mexican Spanish jitomate). If the reviewer wants the generic term, revert to tomatl.
nah.headword: Molina 1571 s.v. xitomatl; cf. Karttunen 1983 (from memory; page not checked)

yua.note: p'aak 'tomato' (Bricker et al. 1998; Diccionario básico). Native word.
yua.headword: p'aak (Bricker et al. 1998) (from memory; page not verified)

quz.note: Reviewer accepted: adapted loan 'tumati' (trivocalic). Tomato word is Nahuatl via Spanish; no native Quechua term known to me.
quz.reviewQuestion: For tomato, do speakers say 'tumati', 'tomate', or another word? Which spelling would you use?

cjp.note: Cultivated tomato has no entry. shalbo names a different wild plant, so it is not offered as the card word. Spanish loan, unattested in Cabécar sources.
cjp.source: no Cabécar term for cultivated tomato in margery1989; wild relative shalbo (d.n., 5985) 'tomate de montaña' (Cyphomandra)

bzd.note: No Bribri entry for tomato. No attested loan found.
bzd.reviewQuestion: Do children in your community use a Spanish loan for this (how is it pronounced/written in Bribri spelling), or is there a Bribri word or phrase?

verso.es:
Redondo, rojo y jugoso,
maduró al sol de la huerta.
verso.en:
Round, red, and juicy,
it ripened in the garden sun.

riddle.es: Soy rojo y jugoso y pongo color a la salsa.
riddle.en: I am red and juicy and I give color to the salsa.

nah.note: chimalli "shield" + xochitl "flower". Commonly cited for sunflower in early colonial botanical sources (Hernández); chimalacatl "shield reed" is another cited form. I have not checked the primary entry myself. Fallback: loanword "girasol".
nah.reviewQuestion: ¿Cómo se dice "girasol" en su variante: chimalxochitl, chimalacatl u otra?

yua.note: Built from attested roots: u (3rd person possessive) + lool 'flower' + k'iin 'sun'. Not an established name. Sunflower is not a traditional peninsular crop; speakers most likely say girasol (Spanish loan), which is a safe alternative. The possessive phrase order should be checked by a speaker. IPA ?.
yua.reviewQuestion: What do you call a sunflower? Would 'u lool k'iin' sound natural, strange, or wrong?

quz.note: Reviewer accepted: adapted loan, no /x/ or o (g→h, o→u), penultimate stress. Sunflower is a North American crop. A coined native phrase like 'inti qhawaq' (inti 'sun' + qhawa- 'look' + -q agentive) is NOT used: invented, and sun-cult flavoured.
quz.reviewQuestion: For sunflower, do speakers say 'hirasul', 'girasol', or a Quechua phrase? Which spelling would you use?

cjp.note: Southern-dialect only; no northern form found. Nasal underlines read from the scan (u, í) — verify.

bzd.note: No Bribri entry for sunflower. Generic 'flower' is attested (dakuà / mà̱ma̱) but would not identify this card. A phrase with dìwö 'sun' would be an invention, so not proposed.
bzd.reviewQuestion: Is there a Bribri name for the sunflower, or a Spanish loan in use? Would 'flower' (dakuà / mà̱ma̱) be acceptable?

verso.es:
Sigue la luz todo el día
con su cara de oro.
verso.en:
It follows the light all day
with its golden face.

riddle.es: Mi cara dorada sigue la luz todo el día y mis pipas son un tesoro para los pájaros.
riddle.en: My golden face follows the light all day, and my seeds are a treasure for the birds.

nah.gloss: sun (lit. 'one who goes along giving warmth/light')
nah.note: Kept existing draft. Molina 'tonatiuh: el sol' is the ordinary Classical noun for the sun. CAUTION: identical to the deity name Tonatiuh. No separate profane noun exists in Classical; tonalli means sun's heat/day but also 'soul, day sign' (more ritual-loaded). Modern varieties use tonati, tonaltzin, etc. Reviewer must decide whether this is acceptable for the card.
nah.reviewQuestion: "Tonatiuh" también es nombre de una deidad. ¿Le parece bien usarlo como la palabra común para "sol" en un juego para niños, o prefiere otra (tonati, tonaltzin…)?
nah.headword: Molina 1571 s.v. tonatiuh; cf. Karttunen 1983 (from memory; page not checked)

yua.note: Kept existing draft. k'iin = sun, day, time (all major dictionaries). Association: K'inich, solar deity; the plain noun is everyday. Respectful address forms (e.g. Yuum K'iin) avoided.
yua.headword: k'iin (Bricker et al. 1998) (from memory; page not verified)

quz.note: Kept existing draft. Everyday word for the sun; also the name of the Inca sun deity (Inti). Card shows the celestial body, which is the ordinary sense. Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976).
quz.headword: inti (AMLQ 2005 / Cusihuamán 1976 headword form, from memory; page not verified)

cjp.note: Bible spelling (MMS training text). Dictionary: ká_ wö́ (general), kö́wö́ and k'á_ wö (d.n.). The sun figures in Cabécar cosmology (Sibö's creation narratives) — neutral as a noun but note for reviewers.
cjp.source: bibleis-cjptjv Mt 24:29, Rev 10:1, Rev 12:1 'ka̱wä'; margery1989 entry 3085 ká_ wö́ 'sol'

bzd.note: Everyday word. Sensitivity: the sun has mythological names (Dalàbulu, Dìwö Akë́köl) and a sun clan (Dìwöwak) — do NOT use those.
bzd.source: jaragarcia2013 (as indexed in Krohn 2025 online dictionary, ES→BRI entry 'sol'; primary page not verified)
bzd.reviewQuestion: Is dìwö correct for the sun picture?

verso.es:
Sale por el este despacito
y pinta de oro la mañana.
verso.en:
It rises slowly in the east
and paints the morning gold.

riddle.es: Cada día salgo y me escondo; sin mí no habría día ni calor.
riddle.en: Every day I rise and hide; without me there would be no day and no warmth.

nah.note: Kept existing draft. Molina 'metztli: luna o mes'. Also the name of a lunar deity in some sources, but primarily the ordinary noun. Sounds close to mixtli (nube); avoidWith set.
nah.headword: Molina 1571 s.v. metztli; cf. Karttunen 1983 (from memory; page not checked)

yua.note: Kept existing draft. uj = moon, month (all major dictionaries). Some speakers use respectful/ritual address forms for the moon; those are avoided here.
yua.headword: uj (Bricker et al. 1998) (from memory; page not verified)

quz.note: Kept existing draft. Moon; also means 'month'. Mama Killa is the moon deity, but 'killa' alone is the everyday noun. Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976).
quz.headword: killa (AMLQ 2005 / Cusihuamán 1976 headword form, from memory; page not verified)

cjp.note: Same in dictionary and Bible. tulu balá = full moon (6730).

bzd.note: Variants si’wö and short si’ (Jara & García list si’ among the forms). Choose one per community.
bzd.source: margery1996; jaragarcia2013; jaragarcia2003 (as indexed in Krohn 2025 online dictionary, ES→BRI entry 'luna'; primary page not verified)
bzd.reviewQuestion: Which form do children use: síwö, si’wö or si’?

verso.es:
Cambia de forma cada noche
y platea el camino.
verso.en:
It changes shape every night
and silvers the path.

riddle.es: Soy redonda, luego una uña; alumbro la noche sin ser lámpara.
riddle.en: I am round, then a fingernail; I light the night without being a lamp.

nah.note: Molina 'citlalin: estrella'; Karttunen citlalin. Modern forms: sitlalin, sitlali.
nah.headword: Molina 1571 s.v. citlalin; cf. Karttunen 1983 (from memory; page not checked)

yua.note: éek' 'star' (Bricker et al. 1998; Diccionario básico). Do not confuse with ek' 'black, dark' in some colonial spellings.
yua.headword: éek' (Bricker et al. 1998) (from memory; page not verified)

quz.note: Standard word for star (AMLQ 'qoyllur'); o allophone before/after q. Also in the pilgrimage name Qoyllur Rit'i; the noun itself is ordinary. Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976).
quz.headword: qoyllur (AMLQ 2005 / Cusihuamán 1976 headword form, from memory; page not verified)

cjp.note: Bible spelling chosen for MMS. Dictionary forms are written as two words (béi wö́ / bék wö́); bekwä appears to be the same word written together.
cjp.source: bibleis-cjptjv Mt 2:2, Mt 24:29, Rev 12:1 'bekwä'; margery1989 entry 312 béi wö́ (d.n.), margery1989 entry 316 bék wö́ (d.s.)

bzd.note: Everyday word.
bzd.source: jaragarcia2013; margery1996 (as indexed in Krohn 2025 online dictionary, ES→BRI entry 'estrella'; primary page not verified)
bzd.reviewQuestion: Is bë̀kwö right?

verso.es:
Un puntito que titila
en la noche, muy lejos.
verso.en:
A tiny dot that twinkles
in the night, very far away.

riddle.es: Brillo de noche en el cielo oscuro y parezco un puntito, pero soy una enorme bola de fuego.
riddle.en: I shine at night in the dark sky and look like a tiny dot, but I am an enormous ball of fire.

nah.note: Molina 'quiahuitl: lluvia'; Karttunen quiyahuitl (also spelled quiyahuitl). Also a day sign; ordinary noun.
nah.headword: Molina 1571 s.v. quiahuitl; cf. Karttunen 1983 (from memory; page not checked)

yua.note: Changed from ja'ajal (reviewer flagged it unverified; it may be the verb 'to rain'). ja'al is offered as the noun 'rain', derived from ja' 'water'; IPA ? and form unverified. Deliberately avoided: cháak, which can mean rain in everyday speech but is also the name of the rain deity (Ch'a' Cháak ceremony); if speakers say cháak for rain a native speaker must decide whether that is acceptable.
yua.reviewQuestion: What is the everyday word for 'rain' (the noun): ja'al, ja'ajal, cháak, or something else? Is cháak acceptable for children, or only for the rain deity?

quz.note: Rain (noun; verb 'para-' to rain). Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976).
quz.headword: para (AMLQ 2005 / Cusihuamán 1976 headword form, from memory; page not verified)

cjp.note: Bible spelling; dictionary accents the second syllable. ka_lí_ bulána 'llover'.

bzd.note: Variant kò̱li̱ (dialectal a/o alternation in nasal syllables).
bzd.source: jara2018; margery1996; constenla1998 (as indexed in Krohn 2025 online dictionary, ES→BRI entry 'lluvia'; primary page not verified)
bzd.reviewQuestion: Which variant is used in your community: kà̱li̱ or kò̱li̱?

verso.es:
Gota a gota cae del cielo
y despierta la semilla.
verso.en:
Drop by drop it falls from the sky
and wakes the seed.

riddle.es: Caigo en gotitas desde las nubes y hago crecer las milpas.
riddle.en: I fall in little drops from the clouds and help the milpas grow.

nah.note: petlani "to flash, shine" with tla- and the -lli patient nominal: tlapetlanilli "something flashed". I believe Molina has related forms (tlapetlaniliztli) for relámpago but I have not verified this exact form. Coined for this deck, not traditional.
nah.reviewQuestion: ¿Cómo se dice "rayo" o "relámpago" en su variante?

yua.note: lelem 'lightning, flash' as I recall it from Cordemex (cf. lemba' 'to shine'); kept as attested only on that recollection, with low confidence: I cannot confirm it is the everyday modern word. IPA ?. Association: lightning is tied to the Chaako'ob (rain deities) and their axes; avoid any form naming them.
yua.reviewQuestion: What do you call a lightning flash in everyday speech? Is 'lelem' right, and is the word connected to the Chaako'ob in a way that should stay off a children's game?
yua.headword: lelem (Cordemex) (from memory; page not verified)

quz.note: Common word for lightning/thunderbolt; also the name of the Inca thunder/weather deity (Illapa) and colloquially 'gun'. Kept because it is the ordinary noun (like inti, killa), but flagged for reviewers. Alternative: 'q'aqya' (thunder / thunderbolt). Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976). Reviewer spells the alternative 'qhaqya' (aspirate); I had 'q'aqya' (ejective) — needs checking.
quz.reviewQuestion: For a lightning bolt, would a child say 'illapa' or 'qhaqya'/'q'aqya'? Is 'illapa' too tied to the old deity or to 'gun' for a children's game?
quz.headword: illapa (AMLQ 2005 / Cusihuamán 1976 headword form, from memory; page not verified)

cjp.note: Northern form. d.s. tala wö́rkua (6435). The Bible renders lightning as 'ka̱ wäju̱r' (Mt 28:3, Lk 10:18), which may be a verb phrase ('it flashes'). Thunder is tala bula (Rev 4:5). Storms/thunder have spiritual associations; neutral as noun.
cjp.reviewQuestion: ¿Para el rayo dicen 'kuálklö', 'tala wörkua' o 'ka̱ wäju̱r'?

bzd.note: Single source: personal communication from Alí García Segura recorded in Krohn's dictionary. Thunder is alá. Sensitivity: thunder/lightning are tied to mythological beings (Kikílma̱, Télma̱, Talàchake, the thunder lords) — do NOT use those names; ritual-speech tkë́rme̱ also avoided.
bzd.source: garcia_com_pers (as indexed in Krohn 2025 online dictionary, ES→BRI entry 'relámpago'; primary page not verified)
bzd.reviewQuestion: Is talàwöñor the everyday word for a lightning bolt? Variant tlàwöñor?

verso.es:
Un destello en la tormenta,
luego el trueno responde.
verso.en:
A flash in the storm,
then the thunder answers.

riddle.es: Soy una línea de luz en la tormenta; primero me ves y luego me oyes.
riddle.en: I am a line of light in the storm; first you see me, then you hear me.

nah.gloss: rainbow (ayahuitl "mist" + cozamalotl; literal sense of the second element uncertain)
nah.note: Molina 'ayauhcoçamalotl: arco del cielo'; ayahuitl 'mist' + cozamalotl. Long for a caller; modern varieties often shorten or use other forms. Literal gloss of cozamalotl is debated.
nah.reviewQuestion: ¿Cómo se dice "arcoíris" en su variante? ¿Se usa "ayauhcozamalotl" o una forma más corta?
nah.headword: Molina 1571 s.v. ayauhcoçamalotl; cf. Karttunen 1983 (from memory; page not checked)

yua.note: PROVISIONAL. chéel 'rainbow' as recalled from Cordemex/Bricker; I am not sure of the form or that it is in everyday use, so confidence is low. Taboo risk: in some communities the rainbow is considered dangerous (said to come out of cenotes, cause illness, not to be pointed at), and it is linked in scholarship with Ix Chel. A speaker must confirm it is acceptable on a children's card.
yua.reviewQuestion: What do you call a rainbow? Is 'chéel' right? Is the rainbow considered dangerous or unlucky, and would it be OK on a children's card?
yua.headword: chéel (Cordemex chel) (from memory; page not verified)

quz.note: Standard word for rainbow. Folk belief: rainbows can cause illness (pregnant women and children are told not to point at it); reviewers may want to note this for children's use. Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976).
quz.headword: k'uychi (AMLQ 2005 / Cusihuamán 1976 headword form, from memory; page not verified)

cjp.note: Bible spelling; d.s. shkabä (also 'halo of sun/moon'). In many Chibchan traditions the rainbow is an omen; check whether it carries a taboo for children.
cjp.reviewQuestion: ¿'Shikaba' es el arcoíris? ¿Tiene algún significado delicado?

bzd.note: Alternatives: tkabë̀ / tkabë̀köl (also 'snake'; Margery) and shkaba’ (Jara & García 2003, mythology dictionary). Sensitivity: in Bribri tradition the rainbow is associated with a serpent; dulà avoids the homonym with 'snake' (also a card). Do not confuse with Dulù (mythological serpent).
bzd.source: margery1996 (as indexed in Krohn 2025 online dictionary, ES→BRI entry 'arcoíris'; primary page not verified)
bzd.reviewQuestion: Which word do children use for the rainbow: dulà, tkabë̀köl or shkaba’? Is any of them sensitive?

verso.es:
Después de la lluvia y el sol,
siete colores hacen un puente.
verso.en:
After the rain and the sun,
seven colors make a bridge.

riddle.es: Salgo cuando llueve y brilla el sol; tengo muchos colores en un arco.
riddle.en: I appear when it rains and the sun shines; I have many colors in an arch.

nah.note: Molina 'mixtli: nube'; Karttunen mixtli.
nah.headword: Molina 1571 s.v. mixtli; cf. Karttunen 1983 (from memory; page not checked)

yua.note: múuyal 'cloud' (Bricker et al. 1998; Diccionario básico).
yua.headword: múuyal (Bricker et al. 1998) (from memory; page not verified)

quz.note: Standard word for cloud (also mist). Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976).
quz.headword: phuyu (AMLQ 2005 / Cusihuamán 1976 headword form, from memory; page not verified)

cjp.note: Same in dictionary and Bible. One-syllable word.
cjp.source: margery1989 entry 4369 (s. cl. pl.) 'nube'; bibleis-cjptjv Mt 24:30, Rev 10:1 'mo̱'

bzd.note: Everyday word; nasal vowel.
bzd.source: jaragarcia2013; margery1996 (as indexed in Krohn 2025 online dictionary, ES→BRI entry 'nube'; primary page not verified)
bzd.reviewQuestion: Is mò̱ right?

verso.es:
Blanda y blanca navega
por el mar de arriba.
verso.en:
Soft and white, it sails
across the sea above.

riddle.es: Floto en el cielo como algodón y guardo agua para la lluvia.
riddle.en: I float in the sky like cotton and keep water for the rain.

nah.note: Molina 'ehecatl: viento'; Karttunen ehēcatl. CAUTION: same form as the wind deity Ehecatl and a day sign; it is the ordinary noun but reviewer should judge, as with tonatiuh. Modern forms: ejekatl, ajakatl.
nah.reviewQuestion: "Ehecatl" también es nombre de una deidad. ¿Le parece bien como palabra común para "viento" en un juego para niños, o prefiere otra forma?
nah.headword: Molina 1571 s.v. ehecatl; cf. Karttunen 1983 (from memory; page not checked)

yua.note: iik' 'wind, breath' (all major dictionaries). Also means spirit/breath and is a day name in the calendar; the everyday sense is wind. Minimal pair with iik 'chile' (plain k) on the chile card.
yua.headword: iik' (Bricker et al. 1998) (from memory; page not verified)

quz.note: Standard word for wind. Note 'wayra' also figures in folk illness concepts ('mal viento'), but the noun is everyday. Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976).
quz.headword: wayra (AMLQ 2005 / Cusihuamán 1976 headword form, from memory; page not verified)

cjp.note: SENSITIVE: si_wá_ also means traditional/sacred knowledge and narratives ('historia', 'leyenda'); using it for wind is normal everyday speech, but reviewers should confirm it is fine on a game card.
cjp.source: margery1989 entry 5682 si_wá_ 'viento', 'aire', 'historia, leyenda'; bibleis-cjptjv Mt 7:25 'si̱wa̱'
cjp.reviewQuestion: ¿'Si̱wa̱' para el viento en un juego infantil está bien, dado que también significa la historia/sabiduría tradicional?

bzd.note: Variants si̱wa̱’, su̱a̱’. Sensitivity: the same form also means 'knowledge' and 'sacred history / traditional narration' (Constenla et al. 1998; Jara & García 2003). Reviewer should confirm it is appropriate as a game word for 'wind'.
bzd.source: jaragarcia2003; constenla1998 (as indexed in Krohn 2025 online dictionary, ES→BRI entry 'viento'; primary page not verified)
bzd.reviewQuestion: Is su̱wa̱’ acceptable for the wind card given its other meaning ('sacred history')? Is there a better everyday word?

verso.es:
No se ve pero se siente,
mueve hojas y plumas.
verso.en:
You cannot see it but you feel it,
it moves leaves and feathers.

riddle.es: No tengo cuerpo pero muevo todo; sopla y me escucharás silbar.
riddle.en: I have no body yet I move everything; listen and you will hear me whistle.

nah.note: citlalin "star" + popoca "it smokes": a clause, "the star smokes". I recall Molina giving this for cometa but cannot confirm the entry, so treated as descriptive. Until verified, treat as coined for this deck, not traditional. Shares citlalin with estrella, so the two must not be offered together.
nah.reviewQuestion: ¿Cómo se dice "cometa" (estrella con cola) en su variante? ¿Se usa "citlalin popoca"?

yua.note: búuts' 'smoke' (long vowel, as in Bricker et al. 1998) + éek' 'star'. Earlier draft wrote short buts'. I believe colonial dictionaries record budz ek for comet, which would make it attested, but I have not verified it, so it is descriptive, low. Alternative: Spanish loan cometa.
yua.reviewQuestion: Is there a Maya word for a comet? Would 'búuts' éek'' (smoke star) be understood, or do people say 'cometa'?

quz.note: Descriptive phrase: chupa 'tail' + -yuq 'possessor' + quyllur 'star'. I could not confirm a traditional single word for comet; colonial lexicons may record one, which reviewers should prefer if found. Could also simply be Spanish 'cometa'.
quz.reviewQuestion: Is there a Quechua word for a comet? Would 'chupayuq quyllur' ('star with a tail') be understood, or would speakers just say 'cometa'?

cjp.note: No word for 'comet' found; this is the southern term for a meteor/shooting star (d.n. equivalent at entry 370, not verified on scan). Bible Mt 24:29 'bekwä jolortémi' = 'stars will fall'. SENSITIVE: the dictionary records fiery streaks in the sky (ja_má_ júr, mit., 1908) as omens of calamity — confirm the shooting-star word is not ominous for children.
cjp.reviewQuestion: ¿Hay palabra para 'cometa'? ¿La estrella fugaz se considera mal presagio?

bzd.note: No Bribri entry for comet. Not inventing a descriptive phrase.
bzd.reviewQuestion: Is there a Bribri name for a comet (or 'star with a tail')? Or a Spanish loan in use?

verso.es:
Con su cola de luz
visita el cielo y se va.
verso.en:
With its tail of light
it visits the sky and leaves.

riddle.es: Soy bola de hielo y polvo con larga cola brillante; vengo de lejos y no me quedo.
riddle.en: I am a ball of ice and dust with a long glowing tail; I come from far and do not stay.

nah.note: Kept existing draft. Molina 'tepetl: monte o sierra'. Shares tepetl with volcan and pueblo (altepetl); avoidWith set.
nah.headword: Molina 1571 s.v. tepetl; cf. Karttunen 1983 (from memory; page not checked)

yua.note: wits (colonial witz) 'hill, mountain' (Cordemex; Bricker). The peninsula is flat; locally the word mostly names hills. Alternative: puuk 'range of hills' (the Puuc). Snowy peaks in the verse have no local referent.
yua.reviewQuestion: Is 'wits' the word for a big mountain, or only for a hill? Would you use puuk?
yua.headword: wits (Cordemex witz) (from memory; page not verified)

quz.note: Plain word for mountain/hill (AMLQ 'orqo'). Deliberately NOT 'apu', which denotes a sacred mountain lord/spirit and is a ritual term. Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976). Note: 'urqu' also means 'male' (of animals, e.g. urqu llama), so it can be heard that way out of context.
quz.headword: orqo (AMLQ 2005 / Cusihuamán 1976 headword form, from memory; page not verified)

cjp.note: Bible spelling. Dictionary: ká_ tsö (s. cl. red.) and ká_ bata (generic). Some mountains (e.g. Chirripó peaks) are sacred places; the generic noun is neutral.
cjp.source: bibleis-cjptjv Mt 5:14, Mt 17:1 'ka̱tsä (bata)'; margery1989 entry 2928 ká_ bata 'cerro, montaña'

bzd.note: Variants ká̱bta, kó̱bata, kó̱bta.
bzd.source: jaragarcia2013 (as indexed in Krohn 2025 online dictionary, ES→BRI entry 'montaña'; primary page not verified)
bzd.reviewQuestion: Which variant is used in your community?

verso.es:
Alta y callada, se pone
un sombrero de nieve.
verso.en:
Tall and quiet, it puts on
a hat of snow.

riddle.es: Soy muy grande y muy alta; de mis laderas bajan los ríos.
riddle.en: I am very big and very tall; rivers run down my slopes.

nah.note: popoca "to smoke" (intransitive verb) + -ni (customary agentive on present stem) gives popocani "one that smokes", used here as a modifier before tepetl "mountain". Classical would more naturally compound verb stem + noun as popocatepetl, but that is the proper name of one volcano, so avoided. Coined for this deck, not traditional.
nah.reviewQuestion: ¿Hay una palabra general para "volcán" en su variante? ¿Se entiende "popocani tepetl" o suena raro?

yua.note: Built from k'aak' 'fire' + -il (relational suffix) + wits 'hill/mountain'. There are no volcanoes on the peninsula and no traditional word is expected; Spanish volcán is the likely everyday form and a safe alternative. Modifier construction needs a speaker's check (k'aak' wits vs k'aak'il wits). IPA ?.
yua.reviewQuestion: How would you say 'volcano'? Would 'k'aak'il wits' (fire mountain) make sense, or do people just say 'volcán'?

quz.note: Descriptive compound: nina 'fire' + urqu 'mountain'. No well-attested Cusco word for volcano known to me (Cusco has no active volcanoes); speakers likely say Spanish 'volcán'. Specific volcanoes (Misti, Sabancaya) are apu-type sacred peaks, so avoid naming one. Reviewers may prefer the loan. Shares 'urqu' with montana (avoidWith); 'urqu' also means 'male'.
quz.reviewQuestion: Is 'nina urqu' ('fire mountain') understood as volcano, or do speakers say 'volcán'/'wulkan'? Does 'urqu' risk being heard as 'male' here?

cjp.note: No native term found. Bible Rev 8:8 describes 'something like a great mountain burning' descriptively. Spanish loan, unattested.
cjp.reviewQuestion: ¿Cómo llaman a un volcán (p. ej. el Turrialba)?

bzd.note: No Bribri entry for volcano (Talamanca has no active volcanoes). Not substituting 'mountain'.
bzd.reviewQuestion: Do children in your community use a Spanish loan for this (how is it pronounced/written in Bribri spelling), or is there a Bribri word or phrase?

verso.es:
Duerme con humo en la cima
y a veces despierta con fuerza.
verso.en:
It sleeps with smoke on top
and sometimes wakes up with force.

riddle.es: Tengo un hueco en la cima y guardo fuego por dentro; a veces echo humo y ceniza.
riddle.en: I have a hollow top and keep fire inside; sometimes I puff out smoke and ash.

nah.note: Molina 'ameyalli: fuente o manantial'; from atl 'water' + meya 'to flow'.
nah.headword: Molina 1571 s.v. ameyalli; cf. Karttunen 1983 (from memory; page not checked)

yua.note: sayab 'manantial, ojo de agua' (Cordemex). Its everyday modern use is uncertain. Alternative culturally central water source: ts'ono'ot 'cenote', but that is a sinkhole, a different referent, and cenotes have strong ritual associations; not used. Lowered to low: I recall sayab from Cordemex but not its modern currency.
yua.reviewQuestion: What do you call a spring where water comes out of the ground? Is 'sayab' a word you know or use?
yua.headword: sayab (Cordemex) (from memory; page not verified)

quz.note: Standard word for spring/well (Spanish 'puquio' derives from it). Springs are often places of offerings and are believed to have spirits; the noun itself is ordinary. Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976).
quz.headword: pukyu (AMLQ 2005 / Cusihuamán 1976 headword form, from memory; page not verified)

cjp.note: Northern form (díglö 'water'; Bible writes diklä). d.s. díglö yölí (1142); Ch. bölë. Bible Jas 3:11 uses a verb phrase 'diklä tsikirke̱ ska'. Springs can be spiritually significant places.
cjp.reviewQuestion: ¿'Díglö tsi̱ní̱' es el ojo de agua/naciente?

bzd.note: Water spring / source. Appears in place names (e.g. Tùm Ajkö̀ Ki̱, Constenla 2010).
bzd.source: margery1996; constenla2010 (as indexed in Krohn 2025 online dictionary, ES→BRI entry 'manantial'; primary page not verified)
bzd.reviewQuestion: Is tù̱m the word for a water spring?

verso.es:
Brota limpia de la tierra,
y así nace un río.
verso.en:
It bubbles up clean from the ground,
and that is how a river begins.

riddle.es: Salgo de la tierra como agua fresca y de mí nace un río.
riddle.en: I come out of the ground as fresh water, and a river is born from me.

nah.note: Molina 'ilhuicaatl: la mar'; ilhuicatl 'sky' + atl 'water'. Alternatives: hueyatl ('great water'), teoatl (has teo- 'divine' element, avoided). Modern speakers may just say hueyatl or loan 'mar'.
nah.reviewQuestion: ¿Cómo se dice "mar" en su variante: ilhuicaatl, hueyatl, "mar" u otra?
nah.headword: Molina 1571 s.v. ilhuicaatl; cf. Karttunen 1983 (from memory; page not checked)

yua.note: k'áak'nab 'sea' (Bricker et al. 1998; Diccionario básico).
yua.headword: k'áak'nab (Bricker et al. 1998) (from memory; page not verified)

quz.note: Commonly used Cusco term for the sea: a hybrid of Spanish 'la mar' and Quechua qucha 'lake, body of water'. Alternative 'mama qucha' ('mother lake') is the colonial term but also names the sea deity Mamaqucha, so avoided as card word. Plain 'qucha' = lake, too broad. Source: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005) (lists lamar qocha).
quz.reviewQuestion: Do you say 'lamar qucha' for the sea? Is 'mama qucha' better or too religious for a children's game?
quz.headword: lamar qocha (AMLQ 2005 / Cusihuamán 1976 headword form, from memory; page not verified)

cjp.note: Bible spelling (dictionary dayë). Same word means 'salt'.
cjp.source: bibleis-cjptjv Acts 27:41, Rev 4:6 'däyë'; margery1989 entry 1040 dayë 'mar', 'sal'

bzd.note: Variants diyë̀, dyë̀. Sensitivity: ritual-speech words for the sea (Dulù, së̀) must NOT be used.
bzd.source: margery1996; sanchez_sf (as indexed in Krohn 2025 online dictionary, ES→BRI entry 'mar'; primary page not verified)
bzd.reviewQuestion: Is dayë̀ right for the sea?

verso.es:
Olas que vienen y van,
sal y espuma en la orilla.
verso.en:
Waves that come and go,
salt and foam on the shore.

riddle.es: Soy azul, salado y muy grande; mis olas llegan hasta la arena.
riddle.en: I am blue, salty, and very big; my waves reach the sand.

nah.note: huaqui "to dry out" (preterit agentive huacqui "dried") + tlalli "land": "dried-up land". Coined for this deck, not traditional. Attested ixtlahuatl means open plain/savanna, not quite desert.
nah.reviewQuestion: ¿Cómo se dice "desierto" (tierra seca con poca lluvia) en su variante?

yua.note: tikin 'dry' + lu'um 'earth, land', both attested. No deserts on the peninsula; not an established term. Spanish desierto is a likely everyday alternative. IPA ?.
yua.reviewQuestion: How would you say 'desert'? Would 'tikin lu'um' (dry land) make sense, or do people say 'desierto'?

quz.note: Descriptive: ch'aki 'dry' + pampa 'plain, open flat land'. Alternative attested 'purun' / 'purun pampa' (wild, uninhabited, uncultivated land) — closer to colonial 'despoblado' than to a sandy desert. No desert in Cusco; reviewers decide.
quz.reviewQuestion: How would you name a sandy desert: 'ch'aki pampa', 'purun', 'purun pampa', or the Spanish word?

cjp.note: The Bible's rendering of Spanish 'desierto' (wilderness). Lit. roughly 'empty/abandoned place'; it does not evoke sand dunes. Long phrase for a card.
cjp.reviewQuestion: ¿Hay una palabra más corta para desierto, o se usaría 'desierto' en español?

bzd.note: No Bribri entry for desert. Attested 'sand' (stsa̱’ña̱) or 'beach/sandy area' (tsà̱itö) would mean something else.
bzd.reviewQuestion: Do children in your community use a Spanish loan for this (how is it pronounced/written in Bribri spelling), or is there a Bribri word or phrase?

verso.es:
Mucho sol y poca agua,
pero la vida encuentra su camino.
verso.en:
Lots of sun and little water,
but life finds its way.

riddle.es: Tengo arena y poca lluvia; mis plantas guardan agua en su panza.
riddle.en: I have sand and little rain; my plants store water in their bellies.

nah.note: Molina 'quauhtla: arboleda o montaña de árboles'; cuahuitl 'tree' + -tla (abundance). Means forest generally, not specifically tropical jungle. Modern varieties: kuoujtla, kuatitla.
nah.reviewQuestion: ¿Cuauhtla sirve para "selva" (bosque tropical con mucha lluvia) o solo para "bosque"?
nah.headword: Molina 1571 s.v. quauhtla; cf. Karttunen 1983 (from memory; page not checked)

yua.note: k'áax 'forest, wild land, monte' (all major dictionaries). Covers scrub forest broadly, not only tall jungle. The verse's monkeys fit (ma'ax 'spider monkey').
yua.headword: k'áax (Bricker et al. 1998) (from memory; page not verified)

quz.note: Reviewer accepted: reduplicated sach'a 'tree, bush' + sach'a ('many trees' → thicket, forest); treated as descriptive, not a dictionary word for rainforest. Alternatives: 'yunka' (warm lowland zone), 'anti' (eastern lowlands; historical, as in Antisuyu).
quz.reviewQuestion: For the tropical rainforest (many trees, rain, monkeys), would you say 'sach'a sach'a', 'yunka', 'anti', or another word?

cjp.note: Northern form; d.s. kal gi_ (2721). ká_ bata 'cerro' also extends to 'monte'.

bzd.note: Variant kñí̱k. Synonym kàlyök ('selva', Margery 1996).
bzd.source: jara2018; jaragarcia2013; margery1996 (as indexed in Krohn 2025 online dictionary, ES→BRI entry 'selva'; primary page not verified)
bzd.reviewQuestion: Is ka̱ñí̱k or kàlyök better for a rainforest picture?

verso.es:
Verde sobre verde, cantos y sombra,
mil vidas entre las hojas.
verso.en:
Green on green, songs and shade,
a thousand lives among the leaves.

riddle.es: Hay muchos árboles, lluvia y monos; mi techo es de hojas.
riddle.en: There are many trees, rain, and monkeys; my roof is made of leaves.

nah.note: Molina 'tehuilotl: cristal'; Sahagún Book 11 describes it among stones. Confident in the word, less in spelling (te- 'stone' + huilotl?).
nah.reviewQuestion: ¿Conoce "tehuilotl" para el cristal de roca? ¿Cómo lo dicen?
nah.headword: Molina 1571 s.v. tehuilotl; cf. Karttunen 1983 (from memory; page not checked)

yua.note: Spanish loan, kept in Spanish spelling per loan policy. Deliberately avoided: sáastun 'clear stone', the divining crystal used by the j-meen (traditional ritual specialist), a sacred object. Also avoided sáasil tuunich 'clear stone' for being too close to it.
yua.reviewQuestion: Do you say 'cristal' for a rock crystal? Is there a Maya word that is NOT the sáastun of the j-meen?

quz.note: Qispi means crystal/glass/transparent stone (AMLQ 'qespi'); homophonous with qispi 'free, saved' (qispi- 'to escape, be saved'), which can be ambiguous. Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976).
quz.reviewQuestion: Does 'qispi' mean a rock crystal to you? Could children confuse it with 'qispi' meaning 'free/saved'?
quz.headword: qespi (AMLQ 2005 / Cusihuamán 1976 headword form, from memory; page not verified)

cjp.note: No native word for crystal/gem found. The Bible uses the Spanish loan 'vidrio' where Spanish has 'cristal'. 'jak' = stone.
cjp.reviewQuestion: ¿Para un cristal de roca usarían 'vidrio', 'jak' u otra palabra?

bzd.note: No Bribri entry for crystal/quartz. SENSITIVITY: the sacred healing stones of Bribri healers (si̱a̱’, and ritual-speech names) are listed under 'piedra' and must NOT be used for a game card. Plain 'stone' ák exists but names a different thing. Wö̀sa̱wa̱k means 'mirror'.
bzd.reviewQuestion: Is there an everyday (non-sacred) word for a clear crystal or quartz? If the only words are sacred, should this card be skipped in Bribri?

verso.es:
Duerme en la roca oscura
y brilla cuando lo alcanza la luz.
verso.en:
It sleeps in the dark rock
and sparkles when light reaches it.

riddle.es: Nazco dentro de las rocas y brillo con la luz; soy duro y transparente.
riddle.en: I grow inside rocks and sparkle in the light; I am hard and clear.

nah.note: Spanish word, not traditional Nahuatl. Replaced the earlier draft anepantla tlalli, which reviewer judged ungrammatical (adverbial anepantla juxtaposed to a noun without a proper construction). I know no reliable single Classical noun for island.
nah.reviewQuestion: ¿Cómo se dice "isla" (tierra rodeada de agua) en náhuatl en su variante?

yua.note: peten 'island' (Cordemex; source of the place name Petén). Well attested historically; reviewers should confirm current everyday use versus Spanish isla.
yua.reviewQuestion: Do people today say 'peten' for an island, or mostly 'isla'?
yua.headword: peten (Cordemex) (from memory; page not verified)

quz.note: Word for island used especially around Lake Titicaca (Puno/Collao); AMLQ lists wat'a 'isla'. Less familiar to speakers far from lakes. Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005).
quz.reviewQuestion: Is 'wat'a' the word you use for an island, or is it only known around Lake Titicaca?
quz.headword: wat'a (AMLQ 2005 / Cusihuamán 1976 headword form, from memory; page not verified)

cjp.note: Bible term; däyë 'sea'. Dictionary only has díglö wöbla (d.s., 1196) 'small river island'.

bzd.gloss: small river islet; also 'plot of land'
bzd.note: Attested only for 'small island formed in a riverbed' (variants dara’, dra’, dta’). The card shows a sea island with palms, so this is a meaning mismatch. Note data’ also = 'dewlap' (Sánchez).
bzd.source: margery1996 (as indexed in Krohn 2025 online dictionary, ES→BRI entry 'isla'; primary page not verified)
bzd.reviewQuestion: Can data’ be used for an island in the sea, or is there another word?

verso.es:
Un pedacito de tierra
con agua por todos lados.
verso.en:
A little piece of land
with water on every side.

riddle.es: Estoy rodeada de agua por todos lados; algunas tienen palmeras.
riddle.en: I am surrounded by water on all sides; some of us have palm trees.

nah.note: Molina 'oztotl: cueva'; Karttunen oztōtl. Caves have ritual significance in Mesoamerica but the noun is ordinary.
nah.headword: Molina 1571 s.v. oztotl; cf. Karttunen 1983 (from memory; page not checked)

yua.note: áaktun (colonial actun) 'cave' (Bricker et al. 1998; Cordemex). Association: caves are traditional offering places and entrances to the underworld in belief; the noun itself is everyday (common in place names).
yua.headword: áaktun (Bricker et al. 1998) (from memory; page not verified)

quz.note: Standard word for cave/rock shelter (also 'machay' in place names). Caves can be associated with ancestors/spirits (and chinkana tunnels), but mach'ay is the ordinary noun. Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976).
quz.reviewQuestion: Do you pronounce the word for cave with an ejective, 'mach'ay'?
quz.headword: mach'ay (AMLQ 2005 / Cusihuamán 1976 headword form, from memory; page not verified)

cjp.note: No clear noun for 'cave' found. Bible Heb 11:38 'ka̱ wäja̱r' / 'ishäkä wäja̱r' may mean 'holes/caves of the earth' but the gloss is uncertain. Caves can be sacred/burial places in Talamanca tradition. Left null.

bzd.note: Variants kó̱uk; synonym úk / ùk.
bzd.source: constenla1998; margery1996; garcia_com_pers (as indexed in Krohn 2025 online dictionary, ES→BRI entry 'cueva'; primary page not verified)
bzd.reviewQuestion: Is ká̱uk or úk used for a cave?

verso.es:
Oscura y fresca, guarda ecos
y murciélagos que duermen.
verso.en:
Dark and cool, it keeps echoes
and sleeping bats.

riddle.es: Entra sin miedo: soy un hueco en la montaña donde el eco juega.
riddle.en: Step in without fear: I am a hollow in the mountain where echoes play.

nah.note: Molina 'comitl: olla'; Karttunen comitl. Related comalli (griddle).
nah.headword: Molina 1571 s.v. comitl; cf. Karttunen 1983 (from memory; page not checked)

yua.note: kum/kuum 'olla' (Cordemex; Diccionario básico). Vowel length uncertain across sources. Related: p'uul 'water jar (cántaro)', a different vessel. IPA ?.
yua.reviewQuestion: What do you call a clay cooking pot: kum or kuum? Is it different from p'uul?
yua.headword: kum (Cordemex) (from memory; page not verified)

quz.note: Standard word for (clay) cooking pot. Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976).
quz.headword: manka (AMLQ 2005 / Cusihuamán 1976 headword form, from memory; page not verified)

cjp.note: Matches the art (clay pot). Generic 'olla' is u_ (7374), a single nasal vowel — too short for a card.
cjp.source: margery1989 entry 3084 (s. cl. red.) 'olla de barro'
cjp.reviewQuestion: ¿'Ká̱ wí̱' es la olla de barro?

bzd.note: Differs from ù 'house' (card 'casa') only by nasality (macron below). Good teaching pair, but audio and spelling must keep them distinct; avoid using these two as each other's distractors without review.
bzd.source: jaragarcia2013; margery1996 (as indexed in Krohn 2025 online dictionary, ES→BRI entry 'olla'; primary page not verified)
bzd.reviewQuestion: Is ù̱ used for a clay pot? Do children clearly distinguish ù̱ (pot) from ù (house)?

verso.es:
De barro y manos hecha,
hierve el caldo con paciencia.
verso.en:
Made of clay and hands,
it simmers the broth with patience.

riddle.es: Soy de barro y estoy en la lumbre; en mí se cocinan los frijoles.
riddle.en: I am made of clay and sit by the fire; beans cook inside me.

nah.note: Molina 'chiquihuitl: cesto o canasta'; source of Mexican Spanish chiquihuite. Alternative petlacalli is a lidded reed box, not a basket.
nah.headword: Molina 1571 s.v. chiquihuitl; cf. Karttunen 1983 (from memory; page not checked)

yua.note: Kept xúuxak over xak: my recollection is that xúuxak is the modern basket word and xak the colonial form (Cordemex xac), but I am not sure; low. Length ?. IPA ?.
yua.reviewQuestion: What do you call a woven basket: xúuxak, xak, or something else? Is the vowel long?
yua.headword: xúuxak (Bricker et al. 1998) (from memory; page not verified)

quz.note: Word for a woven basket (cane/reed) in Cusco dictionaries. Regional alternatives exist (e.g. 'chiwi', 'wayunka' uncertain); reviewers should pick the local everyday word. Sources: Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976); Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005).
quz.reviewQuestion: What do you call a woven basket for carrying fruit: 'isanka', 'chiwi', or another word?
quz.headword: isanka (AMLQ 2005 / Cusihuamán 1976 headword form, from memory; page not verified)

cjp.note: General form. Other baskets: jokóbölo (d.s.), kok'óbölo (d.n.). Bible uses Spanish 'canasta' (Mt 14:20).
cjp.source: margery1989 entry 523 (s. cl. red.) 'canasto'; (s. cl. pl.) 'bolso pequeño'

bzd.note: Variants jkö́, kö́. Also listed as 'ajkö / kö' in the DIPALICORI traditional house dictionary. Other basket word: àba 'canasto' (Margery). Avoid bika’, a ritual basket of healers.
bzd.source: margery1996; jaragarcia2003; dipalicori_casa (as indexed in Krohn 2025 online dictionary, ES→BRI entry 'canasta'; primary page not verified)
bzd.reviewQuestion: Which is the everyday basket word: ajkö́ or àba?

verso.es:
Trenzado con fibras y tiempo,
lleva el mercado en brazos.
verso.en:
Woven from fibers and time,
it carries the market in its arms.

riddle.es: Estoy tejido de fibras; llevo frutas y no me rompo.
riddle.en: I am woven from fibers; I carry fruit and do not break.

nah.note: Molina 'huehuetl: atabal'. The drum used in ceremonial dance, but the instrument noun is ordinary. Alternative teponaztli is the slit drum. Homophone in unmarked spelling with huehue 'old man' is a mild risk.
nah.headword: Molina 1571 s.v. huehuetl; cf. Karttunen 1983 (from memory; page not checked)

yua.note: tunkul / tunk'ul (colonial spelling tunkul) is the hollow-log slit drum (cf. Nahuatl teponaztli). Uncertain: plain vs ejective k, and whether it fits a hand drum. The skin drum is pax/paax in some sources, but paax now commonly means 'music'. Association: used in traditional ceremonies and dances. IPA ?.
yua.reviewQuestion: What do you call a drum like this one (hit with hands or sticks)? Is 'tunkul' / 'tunk'ul' that drum, or only the hollow log drum? Is it tied to ceremonies?
yua.headword: tunkul (Cordemex) (from memory; page not verified)

quz.note: Wankar / wankara = drum (Spanish 'huancar'); attested in colonial and modern dictionaries. Today 'tinya' names the small hand drum, 'wankar' a larger drum; either may be expected. Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976). 'tinya' may be the better everyday word for a small hand drum.
quz.reviewQuestion: For a drum played with hands or sticks, which word do children know: 'wankar', 'tinya', or another?
quz.headword: wankar (AMLQ 2005 / Cusihuamán 1976 headword form, from memory; page not verified)

cjp.note: General form; SJC bak (154). Drums accompany ceremonies and chichadas; neutral as a noun.

bzd.note: Variant sbák; synonym dulë̀ (Rimolo 2007; also 'traditional chicha-festival song' and 'small bird'). DIPALICORI house dictionary lists 'sabák/dulë'. Possible cultural note: drums accompany traditional dances/songs.
bzd.source: margery1996; dipalicori_casa (as indexed in Krohn 2025 online dictionary, ES→BRI entry 'tambor'; primary page not verified)
bzd.reviewQuestion: Is sabák the right word, and is there any ceremonial restriction on the drum?

verso.es:
Pum, pum, pum, late fuerte
y el baile se pone en marcha.
verso.en:
Boom, boom, boom, it beats strong
and the dance gets going.

riddle.es: Me tocan con las manos o palitos y suena pum pum.
riddle.en: They play me with hands or sticks and I go boom boom.

nah.note: Molina 'xamitl: adobe'. I am fairly but not fully sure of this entry; check against Molina directly.
nah.reviewQuestion: ¿Cómo se dice "adobe" (ladrillo de barro y paja) en su variante? ¿Se usa "xamitl"?
nah.headword: Molina 1571 s.v. xamitl; cf. Karttunen 1983 (from memory; page not checked)

yua.note: Spanish loan. Adobe is not a traditional peninsular building material (houses are stone, bajareque/wattle-and-daub, and palm thatch), so no native term is expected. Descriptive alternative for review: luk' tuunich 'mud stone' (luk' 'mud' + tuunich 'stone'), not established.
yua.reviewQuestion: Is there a Maya word for a mud brick, or do people say 'adobe'?

quz.note: Tika = sun-dried adobe brick (verb 'tikay' to make adobes). Not to be confused with t'ika 'flower' (ejective) — reviewers must check pronunciation/orthography carefully. Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976).
quz.headword: tika (AMLQ 2005 / Cusihuamán 1976 headword form, from memory; page not verified)

cjp.note: Adobe construction is not traditional in the region; no term. Left null.
cjp.reviewQuestion: ¿Hay forma de decir 'adobe' o se usaría el español?

bzd.note: No Bribri entry for adobe brick (not a traditional Bribri building material). dö́ means 'mud, clay' — a different thing.
bzd.reviewQuestion: Do children in your community use a Spanish loan for this (how is it pronounced/written in Bribri spelling), or is there a Bribri word or phrase?

verso.es:
Barro y paja bajo el sol
levantan paredes firmes.
verso.en:
Mud and straw under the sun
raise strong walls.

riddle.es: Me hago con barro y paja y me secan al sol; con mis iguales se levanta una pared.
riddle.en: I am made of mud and straw and dried in the sun; with others like me a wall is built.

nah.note: Molina 'icpatl: hilo'; Karttunen icpatl.
nah.headword: Molina 1571 s.v. icpatl; cf. Karttunen 1983 (from memory; page not checked)

yua.note: k'u'uch 'thread, spun cotton' (Bricker et al. 1998; Cordemex). Related: piits' 'cotton' (raw). Glottal placement needs confirmation. Lowered to low: form and glottal placement unverified. IPA ?.
yua.reviewQuestion: What do you call cotton thread: k'u'uch, k'uuch, or something else?
yua.headword: k'u'uch (Bricker et al. 1998) (from memory; page not verified)

quz.note: Standard word for spun thread/yarn. Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976).
quz.headword: q'aytu (AMLQ 2005 / Cusihuamán 1976 headword form, from memory; page not verified)

cjp.note: General form (tulúk = needle). Uj. ja_má_ kséi (1910).
