bzd.note: Means cord/thread/rope (synonyms stsa’, kichà); also the cabuya plant. Sensitivity: Ja̱mù̱ is also the name of a mythological being (owner of traps) per Jara & García 2003 — the common noun should be fine but confirm. Fine cotton thread: suítöm 'cotton cord' (Jara & García 2008).
bzd.source: margery1996; chevrier2017 (as indexed in Krohn 2025 online dictionary, ES→BRI entry 'hilo'; primary page not verified)
bzd.reviewQuestion: Is ja̱mù̱ fine for sewing/weaving thread, or is suítöm better?

verso.es:
Del algodón y la lana
nace el hilo, y del hilo el telar.
verso.en:
From cotton and wool
the thread is born, and from the thread the loom.

riddle.es: Soy largo y fino y paso por la aguja; con mis compañeros se hace la tela.
riddle.en: I am long and thin and go through the needle; with my fellow threads cloth is made.

nah.note: Molina 'acalli: barca, navío o canoa'; atl 'water' + calli 'house'.
nah.headword: Molina 1571 s.v. acalli; cf. Karttunen 1983 (from memory; page not checked)

yua.note: chem 'canoe, boat' (Cordemex; Bricker). Well attested historically; reviewers should confirm everyday use (some speakers may say barco or kanoa for boats).
yua.reviewQuestion: Do people still say 'chem' for a canoe or small boat?
yua.headword: chem (Cordemex) (from memory; page not verified)

quz.note: Wampu = boat/raft in colonial and modern dictionaries; canoe-specific terms are Amazonian. On Lake Titicaca reed boats are 'balsa' (Spanish) or 'tuytu'(uncertain). Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976).
quz.reviewQuestion: For a small boat paddled on a lake, would you say 'wampu', 'balsa', 'tuytu', or another word?
quz.headword: wampu (AMLQ 2005 / Cusihuamán 1976 headword form, from memory; page not verified)

cjp.note: Bible spelling; dictionary kö_no_.
cjp.source: bibleis-cjptjv Mt 13:2, Acts 27:44 'ko̱no'; margery1989 entry 3838 kö_no_ 'bote', 'canoa'

bzd.note: Variants knò̱, ko̱nò̱. Krohn 2016 (lexical acculturation) also lists it; it may be a borrowing (cf. Spanish canoa). Kept as attested.
bzd.source: margery1996; krohn2016 (as indexed in Krohn 2025 online dictionary, ES→BRI entry 'canoa / bote'; primary page not verified)
bzd.reviewQuestion: Is ka̱nò̱ a native word or felt to be a loan? Is it the everyday word?

verso.es:
Un tronco que se volvió barca
y flota en el agua quieta.
verso.en:
A trunk that became a boat
and floats on still water.

riddle.es: Floto sin ruedas y avanzo con remos sobre el lago.
riddle.en: I float without wheels and move with paddles across the lake.

nah.note: Molina 'quauhpantli: puente de madera'; cuahuitl 'wood' + pantli 'row, flag'. Strictly a wooden footbridge; a modern road bridge may be called by loan 'puente'.
nah.reviewQuestion: ¿Cómo se dice "puente" en su variante? ¿Se usa "cuauhpantli" también para puentes que no son de madera?
nah.headword: Molina 1571 s.v. quauhpantli; cf. Karttunen 1983 (from memory; page not checked)

yua.note: Spanish loan, likely the everyday form in a region with few rivers. I could not confirm a native everyday word. Colonial dictionaries may record a term (to check in Cordemex). Do not invent one.
yua.reviewQuestion: Is there a Maya word for a bridge, or do people say 'puente'?

quz.note: Standard word for bridge (as in Q'iswachaka, the woven grass bridge). Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976).
quz.headword: chaka (AMLQ 2005 / Cusihuamán 1976 headword form, from memory; page not verified)

cjp.note: Primary meaning is rope/vine; 'bridge' sense marked p.u. (rarely used) — fits a hanging/rope bridge. Nasal/tone marking not verified on the scan; Bible uses ksa̱ for 'sand' (Mt 7:26), so tone/nasality distinguishes homonyms.

bzd.note: Single source (personal communication). Krohn's Spanish index lists shkë́k for 'puente', but its own Bribri entry for shkë́k means 'standing, upright' — conflicting; chose shkótkö, whose entry explicitly glosses 'puente'.
bzd.source: garcia_com_pers (as indexed in Krohn 2025 online dictionary, ES→BRI entry 'puente'; primary page not verified)
bzd.reviewQuestion: What is the word for a bridge (hanging/rope bridge): shkótkö, shkë́k or another?

verso.es:
Une una orilla con otra
y nadie se queda aislado.
verso.en:
It joins one bank to another
and no one is left alone.

riddle.es: Cruzo ríos y barrancas sin mojarme; las orillas se dan la mano en mí.
riddle.en: I cross rivers and ravines without getting wet; the banks shake hands over me.

nah.note: xicocuitlatl "beeswax" + ocotl "pine torch": "wax torch". Coined for this deck, not traditional. I believe a similar form may occur in colonial texts but cannot cite it. Colonial Nahuatl also borrowed "candela"; modern speakers often say "vela".
nah.reviewQuestion: ¿Cómo se dice "vela" (de cera) en su variante?

yua.note: kib 'wax, candle' (all major dictionaries). Association: candles are central to offerings (e.g. Janal Pixan, Day of the Dead) but the word is everyday.
yua.headword: kib (Bricker et al. 1998) (from memory; page not verified)

quz.note: Spanish 'vela' adapted to Quechua phonology; candles are post-contact. Speakers may also just say 'vela'. Note 'wila' resembles Aymara 'wila' (red/blood). Candles are central in offerings; fine as a household object.
quz.reviewQuestion: For a wax candle, do you say 'wila', 'vela', or something else? Which spelling would you use?

cjp.note: Bible spelling (lamp). General dictionary form tsa_ni_ (7007) 'hule', 'candela', 'luz' — also means rubber/resin.
cjp.source: bibleis-cjptjv Lk 15:8, Rev 4:5 'tsi̱ni'; margery1989 entry 7127 tsini (d.n.) 'candela', 'luz'

bzd.note: Constenla et al. 1998 gloss 'candela'; Margery 1996 'cera' (wax). Alternative akatùwö 'candela, vela' (Chevrier 2017).
bzd.source: constenla1998; margery1996 (as indexed in Krohn 2025 online dictionary, ES→BRI entry 'vela / candela'; primary page not verified)
bzd.reviewQuestion: Which is used for a candle: bùlña̱ or akatùwö?

verso.es:
Una llamita pequeña
alumbra todo el cuarto.
verso.en:
A tiny flame
lights up the whole room.

riddle.es: Soy de cera, tengo un pabilo y doy luz mientras me derrito.
riddle.en: I am made of wax, I have a wick, and I give light while I melt.

nah.note: tla- + tzotzona "to beat, hammer" + -loni (instrumental): "thing for pounding". Coined for this deck, not traditional. tzotzona also means to play a drum, so it clashes with tambor. Alternatives: tepoztlatzotzonaloni (metal pounder), loanword "martillo".
nah.reviewQuestion: ¿Cómo se dice "martillo" en su variante: "martillo" o una palabra náhuatl?

yua.note: Spanish loan, kept in Spanish spelling per loan policy (earlier draft respelling 'martiyo' removed as unsourced). Related native verb: baj 'to hammer, nail in' (Bricker), but I do not know a native tool noun.
yua.reviewQuestion: Is there a Maya word for a hammer, or do people say 'martillo'?

quz.note: Spanish loan; the metal claw hammer is post-contact. I do not know a reliable native term for hammer (hammerstones existed, but I cannot confirm the word), so no native form is proposed.
quz.reviewQuestion: For a hammer, do you say 'martillu' or 'martillo', and is there any native word?

cjp.note: No native term found (dictionary 'martilla' is an animal, kinkajou). Spanish loan, unattested.

bzd.note: No Bribri entry for hammer. Verbs for hitting exist (tö́k, ppö́k) but no noun.
bzd.reviewQuestion: Do children in your community use a Spanish loan for this (how is it pronounced/written in Bribri spelling), or is there a Bribri word or phrase?

verso.es:
Toc, toc, toc, golpea firme
y el clavo se hunde en la madera.
verso.en:
Tap, tap, tap, it strikes firm
and the nail sinks into the wood.

riddle.es: Tengo mango y cabeza dura; golpeo clavos para armar cosas.
riddle.en: I have a handle and a hard head; I hit nails to build things.

nah.note: Molina 'calli: casa'. Also a day sign; ordinary noun. Modern: kali, kalli.
nah.headword: Molina 1571 s.v. calli; cf. Karttunen 1983 (from memory; page not checked)

yua.note: naj/naaj 'house' (all major dictionaries; length varies by source). Alternative: otoch 'home', usually possessed (in wotoch 'my home').
yua.headword: naj (Bricker et al. 1998) (from memory; page not verified)

quz.note: Standard word for house/home. Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976).
quz.headword: wasi (AMLQ 2005 / Cusihuamán 1976 headword form, from memory; page not verified)

cjp.note: Same in dictionary and Bible. Traditional conical house (usulë) is a sacred structure — the generic ju is neutral.
cjp.source: margery1989 entry 2368 (s. cl. pl.) 'casa' (genérico), 'rancho'; bibleis-cjptjv Mt 7:24-27 'ju'

bzd.note: Title word of the DIPALICORI traditional house dictionary. Combining form wé (as in compounds). Do not use chö́we / wéri (cultured/ritual speech). Minimal pair with ù̱ 'pot' (card 'olla').
bzd.source: margery1996; jaragarcia2013; dipalicori_casa (as indexed in Krohn 2025 online dictionary, ES→BRI entry 'casa'; primary page not verified)
bzd.reviewQuestion: Is ù right?

verso.es:
Techo, puerta y ventana,
aquí siempre hay un lugar.
verso.en:
Roof, door, and window,
there is always a place here.

riddle.es: Tengo techo y paredes; adentro se duerme y se comparte.
riddle.en: I have a roof and walls; inside we sleep and share.

nah.note: Molina 'milli: heredad'; Spanish milpa from milpan 'in the field'. Modern speakers may use milpa itself.
nah.headword: Molina 1571 s.v. milli; cf. Karttunen 1983 (from memory; page not checked)

yua.note: kool 'milpa' (all major dictionaries). Spanish milpa is not from Maya (it is from Nahuatl). Association: milpa ceremonies (e.g. jaanli kool) exist but kool itself is ordinary.
yua.headword: kool (Bricker et al. 1998) (from memory; page not verified)

quz.note: Reviewer suggestion partly accepted: changed from 'sara chakra' to plain 'chakra' so it does not repeat 'sara' (maiz card). Kind kept as attested, not descriptive: chakra is a single dictionary word (source of Spanish 'chacra'), used here as an approximate equivalent — Andean chakra is any field, not specifically Mesoamerican maize–bean–squash intercropping.
quz.reviewQuestion: Is 'chakra' a good name for a field where maize, beans and squash grow together, or would you add something (e.g. 'sara chakra')?
quz.headword: chakra (AMLQ 2005 / Cusihuamán 1976 headword form, from memory; page not verified)

cjp.note: General form; d.n. të́i (6519) and ik'uö́ të́i (1611).

bzd.note: Glossed 'sembradío, labranza, milpa'. A Bribri të̀ is a general cultivated plot, not specifically the Mesoamerican maize–bean–squash milpa.
bzd.source: constenla2010; jaragarcia2013 (as indexed in Krohn 2025 online dictionary, ES→BRI entry 'milpa'; primary page not verified)
bzd.reviewQuestion: Is të̀ the right word for a planted field?

verso.es:
Maíz, frijol y calabaza
crecen juntos y se ayudan.
verso.en:
Maize, beans, and squash
grow together and help each other.

riddle.es: Soy un campo donde tres cultivos crecen juntos: maíz, frijol y calabaza.
riddle.en: I am a field where three crops grow together: maize, bean, and squash.

nah.note: tla- + namaca "to sell" + -oyan "place": "place where things are sold". Regular morphology, but not verified as attested or in use. Coined for this deck, not traditional. Alternative: loanword "tienda".
nah.reviewQuestion: ¿Cómo se dice "tienda" (la de la esquina) en su variante?

yua.note: kúuchil 'place' + koonol 'selling' (kon 'to sell'), both attested. Transparent phrase, not confirmed as the usual word; many speakers likely say tienda (Spanish loan), a safe alternative. IPA ?.
yua.reviewQuestion: What do you call the corner shop: 'tienda', 'kúuchil koonol', or something else?

quz.note: Reviewer accepted: changed from 'qhatu', which means market/market stall (Spanish 'cato'), not a neighbourhood shop. Adapted loan per loan policy (ie→i). 'qhatu' remains an option if reviewers prefer a native word with a broader meaning.
quz.reviewQuestion: For a small neighbourhood shop, would you say 'tinda', 'tienda', or 'qhatu'? Is 'qhatu' only a market?

cjp.note: Southern form; no northern form found. Bible uses 'jile watju̱aklä jui' (house of selling, Jn 2:16).

bzd.note: Compound with wé 'house'; dalì = 'cargo, goods'. Listed in Constenla et al. 1998 and in Krohn 2016 (lexical acculturation), i.e. a coined compound, not a loan.
bzd.source: constenla1998; krohn2016 (as indexed in Krohn 2025 online dictionary, ES→BRI entry 'tienda'; primary page not verified)
bzd.reviewQuestion: Is dalì wé what people say for the local shop?

verso.es:
En la esquina abre su puerta
y hay de todo un poquito.
verso.en:
On the corner it opens its door
and has a little of everything.

riddle.es: Estoy en la esquina del barrio y vendo pan, fruta y otras cosas.
riddle.en: I am on the neighborhood corner and sell bread, fruit and other things.

nah.note: tianquiztli is a market, not a town square; the card shows a square with a fountain and benches, so the meaning does not fit well. Alternatives: ithualli (courtyard, patio), loanword "plaza".
nah.reviewQuestion: Para la plaza del centro del pueblo (no el mercado), ¿qué palabra usan: tianquiztli, ithualli, "plaza" u otra?
nah.headword: Molina 1571 s.v. tianquiztli (from memory; page not checked)

yua.note: k'íiwik (colonial kiuic) 'plaza, market' (Cordemex; Bricker). Vowel length and ejective need confirmation. IPA ?.
yua.reviewQuestion: What do you call the town square: k'íiwik, or 'plaza'? Long vowel?
yua.headword: k'íiwik (Cordemex kiuic) (from memory; page not verified)

quz.note: Spanish loan in common use. Native 'pampa' (open flat ground) was used for Inca plazas (Hawk'aypata, Kusipata), but pampa alone means 'plain', so the loan is clearer.
quz.reviewQuestion: For the town square, do you say 'plasa', 'plaza', or 'pampa'? Would you spell it with an initial cluster ('plasa') or another way?

cjp.note: Shortened from the Bible's phrase for 'marketplace/plaza' ('where we gather, where things are sold'). The shortening is mine — reviewers must confirm it stands alone.
cjp.source: bibleis-cjptjv Mt 11:16, Mt 20:3, Acts 17:17 'sa tapanaklä däli watju̱ak shtä ska'
cjp.reviewQuestion: ¿'Sa tapanaklä' se entiende como plaza? ¿O usan 'plaza'?

bzd.note: No Bribri entry for town square/plaza. ù apà / ùjkö mean 'house yard, patio' — not a public square.
bzd.reviewQuestion: Do children in your community use a Spanish loan for this (how is it pronounced/written in Bribri spelling), or is there a Bribri word or phrase?

verso.es:
En el centro del pueblo,
se juntan juegos y charlas.
verso.en:
In the middle of town,
games and chats gather.

riddle.es: Soy un espacio abierto al centro del pueblo; tengo una fuente y bancas.
riddle.en: I am an open space in the middle of town; I have a fountain and benches.

nah.gloss: place where canoes are laid up/moored
nah.note: acalli "canoe" + teca "to lay down" + -oyan "place": "place where canoes are laid up". I suspected a similar Molina entry but cannot confirm. Coined for this deck, not traditional. Alternative: loanword "puerto".
nah.reviewQuestion: ¿Cómo se dice "puerto" (donde llegan y se amarran las barcas) en su variante?

yua.note: Spanish loan, likely the everyday form (cf. place names Puerto Progreso, Puerto Morelos). Descriptive alternative for review: u kúuchil chem 'place of the canoes' (kúuchil 'place' + chem 'canoe'), not established.
yua.reviewQuestion: Is there a Maya word for a harbour, or do people say 'puerto'?

quz.note: Reviewer accepted: spelling decision 'pwirtu' (ue→wi, o→u). Risk: in Andean Spanish 'puerto' also means a mountain pass, so the loan may be heard as 'pass'. Cusco is inland; no traditional word known. Invented 'wampu samana' not used.
quz.reviewQuestion: For a harbour where boats tie up, would you say 'pwirtu', 'puerto', or another word? Would 'puerto' make you think of a mountain pass instead?

cjp.note: Bible term ('where boats arrive'), also used in the place name 'Buenos Puertos'.

bzd.note: No Bribri entry for harbor/port.
bzd.reviewQuestion: Do children in your community use a Spanish loan for this (how is it pronounced/written in Bribri spelling), or is there a Bribri word or phrase?

verso.es:
Aquí descansan las barcas
y el mar toca la puerta.
verso.en:
Here the boats rest
and the sea knocks at the door.

riddle.es: Las barcas llegan a mí a descansar y se amarran con ancla y cuerda.
riddle.en: Boats come to me to rest and tie up with anchor and rope.

nah.note: Molina 'altepetl: pueblo'; atl 'water' + tepetl 'mountain'. Historically a city-state/polity; for a small village calpolli (neighbourhood) is an alternative. Widely used today for 'pueblo'.
nah.headword: Molina 1571 s.v. altepetl; cf. Karttunen 1983 (from memory; page not checked)

yua.note: kaaj/kaj 'town, community' (all major dictionaries; Restall's work on the colonial cah). Length varies by source.
yua.headword: kaaj (Bricker et al. 1998) (from memory; page not verified)

quz.note: Standard word for town/village/settlement (AMLQ 'llaqta'). Also means 'country/people'. Smaller hamlet: 'ayllu' (kin community, socially loaded) — avoided. Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976).
quz.headword: llaqta (AMLQ 2005 / Cusihuamán 1976 headword form, from memory; page not verified)

cjp.note: Bible term for town/city. Dictionary d.n. ju k'ö́lö́ yökö (2408) 'pueblo, ranchería'.

bzd.note: No generic Bribri entry for village/town found; only place names and ká̱ kibí 'city' (Krohn 2016) and ká̱ 'place, land'. ká̱ kibí would name a city, not a village.
bzd.reviewQuestion: What word or phrase is used for a village/community? Would ká̱ kibí be wrong here?

verso.es:
Casas vecinas, voces amigas,
todos se conocen.
verso.en:
Neighboring houses, friendly voices,
everyone knows each other.

riddle.es: Somos muchas casas juntas y nos ayudamos entre vecinos.
riddle.en: We are many houses together and neighbors help one another.

nah.note: tla- + machtia "to teach" + -lo- (impersonal) + -yan "place": "place where people are taught". I believe forms like this are used in bilingual education but cannot cite a source, so not labelled neologism. Coined for this deck, not traditional. Avoided calmecac/telpochcalli (pre-contact institutions with ritual roles).
nah.reviewQuestion: ¿Cómo se dice "escuela" en su variante: tlamachtiloyan, tlamachtilcalli, "escuela" u otra?

yua.note: Changed from descriptive naajil xook. I believe speakers mostly say escuela, and naajil xook is too close to naaj (casa) for a three-choice call. Alternative for review: naajil xook 'house of reading/study' (naaj 'house' + -il + xook 'read, study'), which I believe appears in bilingual-education materials but cannot cite.
yua.reviewQuestion: Do people say 'escuela' in Maya, or 'najil xook' / another phrase?

quz.note: Descriptive compound: yacha- 'know, learn' + -y nominalizer + wasi 'house'. Widely used in Peruvian bilingual education (Ministerio de Educación EIB materials) and historically for the Inca 'yachaywasi'. Everyday speech often uses Spanish loan 'iskuyla'.
quz.reviewQuestion: For school, do children say 'yachay wasi' or 'iskuyla'?

cjp.note: Bible descriptive rendering of 'escuela'. Modern Cabécar communities with MEP schools probably use the Spanish loan 'escuela'; unverified.
cjp.source: bibleis-cjptjv Acts 19:9 'Tirano wa̱ sä yuäklä jui' (Spanish 'escuela de Tirano')

bzd.note: Spelling varies: stsàwöwe (Margery), tsa’wöwe (Jara 2018), jtsàwöwe. Descriptive alternative se’ yawók wé 'house where we learn' (Krohn 2016). Compound with wé 'house'.
bzd.source: margery1996; jara2018 (as indexed in Krohn 2025 online dictionary, ES→BRI entry 'escuela'; primary page not verified)
bzd.reviewQuestion: Which spelling/pronunciation is used locally: stsàwöwe, tsa’wöwe or jtsàwöwe?

verso.es:
Se aprende y se juega,
cada día algo nuevo.
verso.en:
We learn and we play,
something new each day.

riddle.es: Aquí se aprende a leer y a jugar; hay timbre y recreo.
riddle.en: Here you learn to read and to play; there is a bell and recess.

nah.gloss: place where one looks at the stars
nah.note: citlal(in) "star" + tlachia "to look" + -lo- + -yan "place": "place where stars are looked at"; compare tlachialoni "lookout". Coined for this deck, not traditional. Long; loanword "observatorio" is an alternative.
nah.reviewQuestion: ¿Cómo se diría "observatorio" (lugar para mirar las estrellas) en su variante?

yua.note: Spanish loan; modern institution with no traditional word. Kept as loan (not a naajil- phrase, to avoid clashing with naaj on casa). Descriptive alternative for review: naajil u cha'anta'al eek'o'ob 'house where the stars are watched' (cha'an 'to watch', eek' 'star', -o'ob plural), grammar unverified. Note El Caracol at Chichén Itzá is popularly called an observatory, but that name is Spanish.
yua.reviewQuestion: Do people say 'observatorio', or is there a Maya way to say 'a place to watch the stars'?

quz.note: Descriptive: quyllur 'star' + qhawa- 'look, watch' + -na 'instrument/place' + wasi 'house'. Invented for this card, not attested; no institutional neologism known to me. Speakers would likely say 'observatorio'.
quz.reviewQuestion: Would 'quyllur qhawana wasi' ('house for watching stars') be understood as an observatory, or would speakers say 'observatorio'?

cjp.note: No attested term; any phrase would be invented. Left null.

bzd.note: No Bribri entry for observatory or telescope. Not coining a phrase.
bzd.reviewQuestion: Is there a way to say 'observatory' (place to look at stars)? Otherwise skip this card in Bribri.

verso.es:
Un techo que se abre al cielo
para contar estrellas.
verso.en:
A roof that opens to the sky
to count the stars.

riddle.es: Tengo un telescopio y una cúpula; desde aquí se mira el cielo.
riddle.en: I have a telescope and a dome; from here we watch the sky.

nah.note: amoxtli "book, codex" + calli "house": "book house". Transparent compound; I cannot cite traditional or institutional use for "library". Coined for this deck, not traditional. Alternative: amoxpialoyan "place where books are kept".
nah.reviewQuestion: ¿Cómo se dice "biblioteca" en su variante? ¿Se entiende "amoxcalli"?

yua.note: Changed from descriptive naajil ju'un. Modern institution; Spanish biblioteca is the likely everyday form, and the naajil- phrase clashed with naaj (casa). Alternative for review: naajil ju'un 'house of paper/books' (naaj + -il + ju'un 'paper, book'), not established, no institutional source.
yua.reviewQuestion: Do people say 'biblioteca', or a phrase like 'najil ju'un'?

quz.note: Descriptive with a Spanish loan root: liwru (< 'libro') + wasi 'house'. Some EIB/AMLQ neologism lists use other forms (e.g. 'maytu wasi' or 'qillqa wasi'), which I cannot verify; reviewers should replace with any established institutional term. Loan root spelling uncertain: 'liwru' vs 'libru'.
quz.reviewQuestion: For a library, is there an established Quechua term (e.g. from schools or the Academia)? If 'liwru wasi', do you spell it 'liwru' or 'libru'?

cjp.note: No attested term (dictionary has ayë k'uö 'papel, libro' d.n., entry 84, but no 'library'). Left null rather than compose a phrase.

bzd.note: No Bribri entry for library. Attested parts exist (uyë́jkuö 'book/paper'; X + wé 'house of X' as in dalì wé 'shop', stë̀ wé 'museum'), but no speaker-attested compound for 'library', so none is proposed.
bzd.reviewQuestion: Would uyë́jkuö wé ('book house') be natural for 'library', or is there an existing word?

verso.es:
Mil historias en fila,
esperando una mano que las abra.
verso.en:
A thousand stories in a row,
waiting for a hand to open them.

riddle.es: Tengo estantes llenos de cuentos; se habla bajito y se llevan libros prestados.
riddle.en: I have shelves full of stories; we speak softly and borrow books.
